b: Forms arise from quantities, qualities, boundaries, and limitations, all of which belong to created bodies.

f: What does it mean that Allah is not "limited" (lā maḥdūd)?
b: It means Allah has no boundary, end, or restriction, because boundaries belong to finite quantities and created things.

f: What does it mean that Allah is not "countable" (lā maʿdūd)?
b: It means Allah is not subject to numerical quantity or plurality, because numbers and quantities are characteristics of created things.

f: Why is Allah not divisible or composed of parts?
b: Anything composed of parts depends upon those parts for its existence, and dependence contradicts the necessity of Allah's existence.

f: Why is Allah not finite (lā mutanāhī)?
b: Finiteness belongs to quantities and numbers, while Allah is beyond all limitation and measurement.

f: Why is Allah not described with māhiyyah (whatness)?
b: Asking "what is He?" seeks to place something into a category or genus. Allah is not part of any genus and cannot be composed of a genus and distinguishing feature.

f: Why is Allah not described by physical qualities (kayfiyyah)?
b: Qualities such as color, taste, smell, heat, coldness, moisture, and dryness belong to bodies and created compositions, while Allah is transcendent above them.

f: Why can Allah not be located in a place?
b: A place requires extension and dimensions. Allah is free from dimensions, extension, and spatial containment.

f: What is the difference between being spatially located (mutamakkin) and merely being in a direction or position (mutahayyiz)?
b: Being spatially located requires occupying a measurable place, while spatial orientation is a broader concept. Allah is free from both.

f: Why is Allah not subject to time?
b: Time is a measure of changing events and movement. Allah does not undergo change, succession, or alteration, so time does not apply to Him.

f: Why did al-Taftazani رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ mention many similar statements of Allah's transcendence?
b: To clarify and emphasize Allah's perfection, refute anthropomorphists and misguided sects, and establish the doctrine of divine transcendence in a detailed manner.

f: What is the foundation of denying bodily attributes from Allah according to al-Taftazani رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: The foundation is that bodily characteristics imply possibility, dependence, limitation, and createdness, all of which contradict Allah's necessary existence.

f: What weak arguments did some theologians use to prove Allah is not a body?
b: They argued using linguistic meanings of terms like "body", "substance", and "accident", but these arguments are weaker than the argument based on the impossibility of dependence and limitation for Allah.

f: Why would a composed being not be Allah according to the theologians?
b: If Allah were composed of parts, either those parts would possess divine perfection (leading to multiple necessary beings) or they would lack perfection (making Allah dependent and imperfect).

f: Why can Allah not possess every possible form and quality?
b: Possessing all forms and qualities would require opposites to exist together, such as opposite colors and shapes, which is impossible.

f: Why can Allah not possess only some particular form or quality?
b: Because choosing one possibility over another requires a determiner, which would make Allah dependent and therefore created.

f: How do anthropomorphists argue for bodily attributes of Allah?
b: They rely on texts that apparently mention direction, body, form, or limbs, and argue that every existent must either connect to another thing or be separate from it.

f: How does al-Taftazani رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to anthropomorphic arguments?
b: He says these arguments wrongly apply the rules of physical things to Allah. The rational proofs establish Allah's transcendence, and scriptural texts must either be entrusted to Allah's knowledge or interpreted appropriately.

f: What are the two approaches of Ahl al-Sunnah regarding ambiguous texts about Allah's attributes?
b: The approach of many early scholars is to consign their exact meaning to Allah (tafwīḍ), while many later scholars interpret them with appropriate meanings (taʾwīl) to refute misunderstandings.

f: What does the statement "Nothing resembles Him" (lā yushbihuhu shayʾ) mean?
b: It means nothing shares Allah's reality, perfection, or attributes in a way that makes it comparable to Him.

f: Why can no created thing resemble Allah?
b: Because created attributes such as knowledge and power are limited and dependent, whereas Allah's attributes are perfect, unlimited, and incomparable.

f: What did the author of al-Bidāyah say regarding the difference between human knowledge and Allah's knowledge?
b: He said that human knowledge is an existent, an accident, created, possible, and renewed at every moment. If we affirm knowledge as an attribute of Allah, then Allah's knowledge is existent, an attribute, eternal, necessary, and everlasting from pre-eternity to eternity. Therefore, Allah's knowledge does not resemble the knowledge of creation in any way.

f: According to the author of al-Bidāyah, when is true resemblance (mumاثَّalah) established between two things?
b: True resemblance is established only when two things share all qualities. If they differ in even one attribute, complete resemblance does not exist.

f: What clarification did Shaykh Abū al-Muʿīn al-Nasafī give regarding resemblance (mumاثَّalah)?
b: He explained that resemblance does not require equality in every possible aspect, but rather equality in the specific aspect being compared. For example, two people may be called alike in knowledge of jurisprudence even if they differ in many other qualities.

f: How did Shaykh Abū al-Muʿīn explain the prophetic statement "الْحِنْطَةِ بِالْحِنْطَةِ مِثْلًا بِمِثْلٍ" (wheat for wheat, like for like)?
b: He explained that the resemblance mentioned refers only to equality in measure, not equality in every characteristic, such as weight, number of grains, hardness, or softness.

f: How should the statement of al-Ashʿarī that there is no resemblance except through equality in all respects be understood?
b: It should be understood as referring to equality in all respects relevant to the specific comparison, not every possible attribute.

f: Why does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say that complete equality in every attribute would actually eliminate distinction between two things?
b: Because if two things were identical in every respect, they would not truly be two separate entities. Therefore, complete equality cannot be the meaning of resemblance between distinct beings.

f: Does anything escape Allah's knowledge and power?
b: No. Nothing escapes Allah's knowledge or power. Allah knows everything and has power over everything.

f: Why is ignorance of some things or inability over some things impossible for Allah?
b: Because ignorance and inability are deficiencies and imply dependence upon something that determines or limits Him, which is impossible for Allah.

f: Which groups denied the complete scope of Allah's knowledge or power?
b: Some philosophers claimed Allah does not know particulars and cannot create more than one thing. The Dahriyyah claimed Allah does not know His own essence. Al-Naẓẓām claimed Allah cannot create ignorance or evil. Al-Balkhī claimed Allah cannot create something equivalent to the acts of humans. Many Muʿtazilites claimed Allah cannot create the very acts that humans are capable of.

f: What does the statement "Allah has attributes" mean?
b: It means Allah possesses real attributes such as knowledge, power, and life, which are additional meanings beyond merely saying that Allah exists necessarily.

f: Why do the attributes of Allah not consist merely of names without realities?
b: Because describing Allah as "Knowing" requires the reality of knowledge, and describing Him as "Powerful" requires the reality of power. This is like saying "black" while denying the existence of blackness, which is impossible.

f: What evidence proves that Allah possesses knowledge and power besides the names themselves?
b: The perfectly ordered and precise creation is evidence of Allah's knowledge and power, not merely the use of titles such as "Knowing" and "Powerful."

f: What is the position of the scholars of kalām regarding Allah's life and knowledge?
b: They affirm that Allah is Living and possesses eternal life, and that He is Knowing with eternal, all-encompassing knowledge. These attributes are neither accidents nor impossible to remain.

f: Are Allah's attributes acquired (muktasabah) or necessary?
b: Allah's attributes are neither acquired nor necessary in the sense of being learned through experience. They are eternal attributes belonging to His essence.

f: What is the difference between human knowledge and Allah's knowledge according to Ahl al-Sunnah?
b: Human knowledge is created, temporary, dependent, and acquired, whereas Allah's knowledge is eternal, inherent, all-encompassing, and independent.

f: Why do Ahl al-Sunnah reject the Muʿtazilah claim that Allah is Knowing without possessing knowledge?
b: Because it is contradictory. Saying "He is Knowing" while denying the existence of knowledge is like saying "He is black" while denying blackness.

f: What does the existence of Allah's attributes indicate about the relationship between Allah and creation?
b: Allah's attributes are real and eternal, but they do not resemble created attributes. Allah possesses knowledge and power in a manner befitting His perfection, unlike creation.

f: What is the difference between human knowledge and Allah's knowledge according to Ahl al-Sunnah?
b: Human knowledge is an accident that exists in a created being, is additional to that being, and is created. Allah's knowledge is an eternal attribute that exists with His essence and is not created.

f: Which groups denied that Allah has eternal attributes distinct from His essence?
b: The philosophers and the Muʿtazilah denied that Allah has attributes additional to His essence.

f: How did the philosophers and Muʿtazilah explain Allah's attributes?
b: They claimed that Allah's attributes are identical to His essence. They said Allah's essence is called "Knowing" due to its relation to objects of knowledge and "Powerful" due to its relation to things under His power.

f: Why did the philosophers and Muʿtazilah reject separate attributes for Allah?
b: They feared that affirming eternal attributes would lead to multiple eternal beings or multiple necessary existents besides Allah.

f: How does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ respond to the argument that eternal attributes lead to multiple eternal beings?
b: He responds that what is impossible is multiple eternal divine essences, not Allah possessing eternal attributes. Attributes do not constitute separate independent beings.

f: What problem does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say results from the Muʿtazilah view that attributes are identical with Allah's essence?
b: It would require absurd consequences, such as knowledge itself being power, life, a knower, living, powerful, creator of the universe, and worshipped by creation.

f: Why must Allah's attributes be eternal (azaliyyah)?
b: Because Allah's attributes cannot be created after Him. A created attribute would require change occurring in Allah's essence, which is impossible.

f: What was the position of the Karrāmiyyah regarding Allah's attributes?
b: They affirmed that Allah has attributes but claimed that these attributes are created, because they believed eternal created attributes could not exist with Allah.

f: Why does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say Allah's attributes must be "established in His essence" (qā'imah bi dhātihi)?
b: Because an attribute of something can only be an attribute if it exists with that thing. It cannot truly be an attribute if it exists completely separate from it.

f: What was the Muʿtazilah position regarding Allah's speech?
b: They claimed Allah speaks through speech that exists in something else, denying that speech is an attribute established in Allah's essence.

f: Why did the Muʿtazilah argue that affirming eternal attributes violates tawḥīd?
b: They argued that if attributes are eternal and separate from Allah's essence, then there would be multiple eternal beings and multiple necessary existents.

f: How does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ answer the claim that Allah's attributes create multiple eternal beings?
b: He explains that Allah's attributes are neither identical to His essence nor separate from it. Therefore, there is no plurality of independent eternal beings.

f: What does the statement "Allah's attributes are neither He nor other than Him" mean?
b: It means Allah's attributes are not identical to His essence, but they are also not separate entities independent from Him.

f: Why is the Christian belief in the Trinity different from the Sunni understanding of Allah's attributes?
b: Christians affirmed separate hypostases (aqānīm) of existence, knowledge, and life, treating them as distinct realities. Ahl al-Sunnah affirm attributes without making them separate beings.

f: What are the three hypostases (aqānīm) according to Christian theology mentioned by al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: They are existence, knowledge, and life, which Christians refer to as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

f: Why does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ mention the Christian belief regarding the transfer of the "hypostasis of knowledge" to Jesus عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ?
b: To show that their belief implies that these hypostases are separate entities capable of separation and movement, unlike Allah's attributes.

f: What clarification does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ give regarding the impossibility of multiple eternal beings?
b: The impossibility concerns multiple independent eternal essences, not the existence of eternal attributes belonging to one eternal essence.

f: Why does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ say it is incorrect to say Allah's attributes are individually "necessary existents by themselves"?
b: Because only Allah's essence is necessary by itself. The attributes are necessary through Allah, not independently from Him.

f: How can Allah's attributes be eternal without being separate gods?
b: Because they are eternal while being dependent upon and established in Allah's eternal essence. Not everything eternal must be divine.

f: Why does al-Taftazānī رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ avoid saying simply "there are multiple eternals"?
b: Because this phrase may wrongly suggest that Allah's attributes are independent beings possessing divinity. Instead, one should say Allah is eternal with His attributes.

f: What positions did different theological schools adopt regarding Allah's attributes?
b: The Muʿtazilah and philosophers denied real attributes. The Karrāmiyyah denied their eternality. The Ashʿarīs denied that the attributes are either identical with Allah's essence or completely separate from it.

f: What objection is raised against saying Allah's attributes are "neither identical nor other than Him"?
b: The objection is that this appears to deny both alternatives. If something is not identical to another thing, it should be other than it; and if it is not other, it should be identical.

f: How do Ashʿarīs respond to the objection that "neither identical nor other" is contradictory?
b: They define "otherness" as two things being capable of existing separately from one another. Allah's attributes are not separate from His essence, so they are not "other" in this sense.

f: According to the Ashʿarī explanation, why are Allah's attributes not considered separate entities?
b: Because Allah's attributes cannot exist independently without Allah's essence. They are inseparable from Him.

f: What does the author mean when he says that the knowledge of Allah's attributes is not like the knowledge of creation?
b: Human knowledge is an accident (ʿaraḍ), created, possible in existence, and renewed at every moment. If we affirm knowledge as an attribute of Allah, then Allah's knowledge is an eternal attribute, existing with His essence, necessary, and everlasting from pre-eternity to eternity. Therefore, it does not resemble the knowledge of creation in any way.

f: According to Abū al-Muʿīn al-Nasafī, when can two things be called "similar" (mithl) in language?
b: He argues that in ordinary language two things may be called similar if they share a particular quality. For example, Zayd may be called like ʿAmr in knowledge or jurisprudence even if they differ in many other ways.

f: How does the Ashʿarī interpretation understand similarity (mumاثَّala) between two things?
b: Similarity means equality in all aspects in which the comparison is being made. It does not mean absolute equality in every conceivable respect.

f: Why does the author say that Allah cannot be compared to creation?
b: Because nothing can replace Allah or share His qualities. His attributes such as knowledge and power are infinitely greater and higher than those found in creation, with no true resemblance between them.

f: What does the phrase "Nothing escapes His knowledge and power" mean?
b: It means Allah's knowledge encompasses everything and His power extends over everything. This rejects views such as the philosophers who claimed Allah does not know particulars, and groups who limited His power.

f: Which groups did the author mention as limiting Allah's knowledge or power?
b: The philosophers claimed Allah does not know particulars. The Dahriyyah claimed Allah does not know His own essence. Al-Naẓẓām claimed Allah cannot create ignorance or evil. Al-Balkhī claimed Allah cannot create things like human actions. Many Muʿtazilah claimed Allah cannot create the same things humans are capable of creating.

f: Why does the author affirm that Allah has attributes?
b: Because Allah is described as knowing, powerful, living, and so on. The derived names imply the existence of the meanings from which they are derived. A person cannot truly be called "knowing" without knowledge, just as something cannot be called "black" without blackness.

f: What was the position of the Muʿtazilah and philosophers regarding Allah's attributes?
b: They claimed Allah's attributes are identical with His essence. They interpreted "Allah is knowing" to mean that His essence itself is related to knowledge, not that He possesses a distinct eternal attribute of knowledge.

f: How does the author respond to the claim that affirming attributes requires multiple eternal beings?
b: The impossibility is in having multiple eternal independent essences, not in having one eternal essence with eternal attributes. Therefore, affirming attributes does not contradict tawḥīd.

f: What contradiction does the author say follows from denying Allah's attributes?
b: If knowledge, for example, is identical with Allah's essence, then knowledge would also have to be power, life, being knowledgeable, being alive, and creating the universe, which is impossible.

f: What is the meaning of Allah's attributes being "eternal" (azaliyyah)?
b: It means they have no beginning and were not preceded by non-existence. They are not newly created attributes.

f: What does it mean that Allah's attributes are "established in His essence" (qā'imah bi dhātihi)?
b: It means Allah's attributes exist with Him and are not separate entities existing elsewhere.

f: How did the Muʿtazilah argue against eternal attributes?
b: They argued that affirming eternal attributes separate from Allah's essence would lead to multiple eternal beings and destroy tawḥīd.

f: How do the Ashʿarīs answer the objection that attributes create multiple eternals?
b: They say Allah's attributes are neither identical to His essence nor separate from it. They are eternal attributes belonging to Allah without being independent eternal entities.

f: Why does the author mention the Christians when discussing eternal attributes?
b: Because Christians affirmed multiple eternal realities (such as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). The author distinguishes the Islamic doctrine by saying Allah's attributes are not separate eternal beings.

f: What distinction does the author make between "multiple eternal essences" and "multiple attributes"?
b: Multiple eternal independent essences are impossible, but one eternal essence having multiple attributes does not create multiple gods or independent beings.

f: Why should one avoid saying "the eternal ones" when referring to Allah and His attributes?
b: Because it may cause people to misunderstand that each attribute is an independent entity possessing divinity. The correct expression is that Allah is eternal with His attributes.

f: What does it mean that Allah's attributes are "not Him and not other than Him" (lā huwa wa lā ghayruhu)?
b: It means His attributes are not identical with His essence, but they are also not separate entities independent of His essence. They occupy a position unlike ordinary created things.

f: How do the scholars respond to the objection that "not identical and not other" is impossible because there are only two options?
b: They explain that "otherness" means something whose existence can be separated from another. Allah's attributes are not separable from His essence, so they are neither identical nor separate in that sense.

f: Why does the author compare Allah's attributes to a part and a whole?
b: To show that something can differ in concept from another thing without being completely separate from it. A part is not identical to the whole, but it is also not independent from it.

f: What objection does the author raise against the definition of "otherness" as possible separation?
b: If possible separation alone defines otherness, then the world and Allah would not be different, because the world cannot exist without Allah. Likewise, an accident cannot exist without its subject, yet they are still distinct.

f: What problem arises if one says that only one-sided separation is enough for otherness?
b: Then the part and whole, and essence and attribute, would become separate things, because the part can exist conceptually without the whole and the essence can exist without a particular attribute.

f: What do the scholars mean when they say Allah's essence and attributes are eternal together?
b: They mean Allah's essence has always existed with His attributes. Since Allah is eternal, His attributes are also eternal and cannot be absent from Him.

f: What criticism does the author make of the argument that eternal attributes cannot be "other" than Allah?
b: He argues that the reasoning is not fully consistent because similar reasoning would imply that created things dependent on others are not distinct, whereas scholars agree they are distinct.

f: What is the final conclusion regarding Allah's attributes?
b: Allah has eternal attributes that are established with His essence. They are not identical with His essence, nor are they independent beings separate from Him. This preserves both affirmation of divine attributes and the oneness of Allah.

f: Why do some theologians say Allah's attributes are neither He nor other than Him?
b: They mean that Allah's attributes are not identical with His essence in concept, nor are they separate entities independent from His essence in existence.

f: What objection is raised against interpreting "not other than Him" as merely meaning "not separable in existence"?
b: This interpretation does not work for created accidents and their subjects. For example, an accident exists only with its subject, yet it is still considered distinct from it.

f: What problem arises if "otherness" is defined through relation (iḍāfah)?
b: It would require denying distinction between all relational pairs, such as father and son, brothers, cause and effect, and even all different things, because "other" itself is a relational term.

f: How might someone explain "the attributes are neither Allah nor other than Him" through the relationship between subject and predicate?
b: They may argue that predicates such as "knowing" and "powerful" share existence with the subject while differing in meaning, like saying "the human is a writer."

f: Why does the author reject applying this explanation to knowledge and power?
b: Because this explanation applies to derived descriptions like "knowing" and "powerful" in relation to Allah's essence, not to the actual attributes of knowledge and power themselves, which are the subject of discussion.

f: What example does the author give of something that differs in concept but is not a separate entity?
b: He mentions parts such as one individual from the number ten or the hand of Zayd.

f: What did Abū al-Muʿīn al-Nasafī mention regarding considering a part separate from the whole?
b: He stated that no theologians held that the individual parts of ten or Zayd's hand are completely other than the whole except Jaʿfar ibn Ḥārith, and the others considered this view incorrect.

f: Why did Abū al-Muʿīn reject saying that one part of ten is completely other than ten itself?
b: Because the number ten refers to the collection of all its individual parts. If one part were completely other than ten, it would become other than itself since it is included within ten.

f: Why did Abū al-Muʿīn reject saying that Zayd's hand is completely other than Zayd?
b: Because the hand is part of Zayd, so making it completely other would imply that the hand is other than itself.

f: What criticism does the author make of this argument?
b: He says that this reasoning is weak because being a part of something does not remove distinction between the part and the whole.

f: What is the attribute of knowledge (ʿilm) according to the author?
b: Knowledge is an eternal attribute of Allah through which known things become disclosed when the attribute relates to them.

f: What is the attribute of power (qudrah) according to the author?
b: Power is an eternal attribute through which Allah brings possible things into existence when it relates to them.

f: What is the attribute of life (ḥayāh) according to the author?
b: Life is an eternal attribute that makes knowledge possible. A living being is qualified to possess knowledge.

f: What is the meaning of Allah's attribute of strength (quwwah)?
b: It has the same meaning as power (qudrah).

f: What is Allah's attribute of hearing (samʿ)?
b: It is an eternal attribute through which Allah relates to and knows all things that can be heard.

f: What is Allah's attribute of seeing (baṣar)?
b: It is an eternal attribute through which Allah perceives visible things completely, without imagination, assumption, physical senses, or the need for air transmission.

f: Does the eternity of Allah's hearing and seeing require that all sounds and visible things are eternal?
b: No. Just as Allah's eternal knowledge and power do not require that all known things and created things are eternal, His hearing and seeing are eternal while their objects can be created.

f: How do Allah's eternal attributes relate to created things?
b: The attributes are eternal, but their connections (taʿalluqat) with created things occur according to the existence of those things.

f: What are Allah's attributes of will (irādah) and volition (mashīʾah)?
b: They are expressions for an eternal attribute in the living being that specifies one possible thing over another and one time over another, even though Allah's power is equally related to all possibilities.

f: How is Allah's will different from His knowledge?
b: Allah's knowledge follows what occurs, while His will specifies and determines what occurs.

f: What does the author say regarding those who claim Allah's will is eternal but His irādah is created and exists in His essence?
b: He rejects this view because it implies that a created attribute occurs in Allah's essence, which is impossible.

f: How does the author explain Allah's will regarding His own actions?
b: Allah's will for His own actions means that He acts without being forced, distracted, forgetful, or overcome by another.

f: How does the author explain Allah's will regarding the actions of others?
b: Allah's will regarding others' actions means His command and instruction. However, this does not mean that everything He commands necessarily occurs, because He commands all legally responsible people to believe even though some do not.

f: What example does the author give to show that Allah's command does not always mean His will of occurrence?
b: Allah commands every legally responsible person to believe and perform obligations, yet not everyone believes. If command always meant will of occurrence, everyone would necessarily believe.

f: What is meant by Allah's attribute of action and creation (al-fiʿl wa al-takhlīq)?
b: It refers to an eternal attribute called takwīn (bringing into existence/creating). The author avoids using only the word "creation" because it is commonly used to refer to the created thing itself.

f: What is the attribute of takwīn (formation/bringing into existence)?
b: It is an eternal attribute established in Allah's essence through which acts such as creating, providing sustenance, shaping, giving life, and causing death are connected to Allah.

f: Why does the author mention provision (tarzīq) separately after creation?
b: To clarify that acts such as creating, providing sustenance, forming, giving life, and causing death all return to one real eternal attribute: takwīn.

f: What view does the author attribute to al-Ashʿarī regarding Allah's actions?
b: He attributes to al-Ashʿarī the view that Allah's actions are not based on an eternal attribute of takwīn, but rather are understood through relationships (iḍāfāt) and attributes connected to actions.

f: What is the author's position regarding Allah's actions?
b: He holds that Allah's actions are based on a real eternal attribute established in Allah's essence, namely takwīn.

f: What is Allah's attribute of speech (kalām)?
b: Speech is an eternal attribute of Allah. It is expressed through the wording and arrangement known as the Qur'an, which is composed of letters.

f: Why does the author argue that speech is not the same as knowledge?
b: Because a person may speak about something he does not know, or even say something contrary to what he knows. Therefore, speech and knowledge are distinct meanings.

f: Why does the author argue that speech is not the same as will?
b: Because a person may command something that he does not actually desire, such as a master commanding his servant in order to test him or reveal his disobedience.

f: What example does the author give to show that speech can differ from will?
b: A person may command his servant to do something while intending that the servant disobey, so the command exists even though the desired action does not.

f: What is meant by "speech of the soul" (kalām nafsī)?
b: It refers to the inner meaning or intention present within the speaker before it is expressed through words, writing, or signs.

f: What poetic line does the author quote regarding inner speech?
b: He quotes al-Akhṭal: "Indeed, speech is in the heart; the tongue was only made as a guide to what is in the heart."

f: How does the author explain the phrase "there is speech in my soul"?
b: People commonly say "there is speech within myself that I want to tell you," showing that speech can refer to an internal meaning before outward expression.

f: What distinction does the author make between internal speech and spoken words?
b: Internal speech is the meaning existing in the soul, while spoken words are expressions that indicate and communicate that meaning.

f: Why does the author say Allah's speech cannot be reduced to knowledge or will?
b: Because speech has its own meaning: commanding, forbidding, informing, and expressing. These functions are not identical to knowledge or will.

f: What evidence does the author give for affirming Allah's attribute of speech (kalām)?
b: The evidence is the consensus of the Muslim ummah and the continuously transmitted reports from the prophets that Allah is a speaker. It is also impossible for speech to exist without an attribute of speech.

f: How many eternal attributes of Allah does the author mention?
b: He mentions eight: knowledge (ʿilm), power (qudrah), life (ḥayāh), hearing (samʿ), seeing (baṣar), will (irādah), creation/bringing into existence (takwīn), and speech (kalām).

f: Why does the author repeatedly emphasize Allah's will, takwīn, and speech?
b: Because these three attributes have greater disagreement and subtlety among theologians, so he gives additional emphasis to proving them.

f: What does the author mean by saying Allah is "One who speaks through speech that is His attribute"?
b: It means Allah is truly described as speaking because He possesses the attribute of speech. This refutes the claim that Allah speaks through a speech that exists separately from Him.

f: How does this refute the Muʿtazilah view of Allah's speech?
b: The Muʿtazilah claimed Allah is called "Speaker" because He creates speech in something else, while speech is not an attribute established in Allah Himself. The author rejects this because a derived description requires the underlying quality to exist in the described entity.

f: Why is Allah's speech described as eternal (azalī)?
b: Because created things cannot occur within Allah's essence. If speech were created and originated after not existing, it would require a change in Allah's essence.

f: What does the author mean by saying Allah's speech is not from the category of letters and sounds?
b: He means Allah's eternal speech is not composed of created sounds and letters, because sounds and letters are temporal occurrences.

f: Why does the author argue that letters and sounds cannot be eternal?
b: Because letters occur sequentially: the second letter cannot be pronounced until the first letter has ended. Anything dependent on the ending of something before it is created cannot be eternal.

f: Which groups does the author say held that Allah's speech consists of eternal letters and sounds?
b: He attributes this view to the Ḥanbalīs and the Karrāmiyyah, who said Allah's speech is an eternal accident consisting of sounds and letters.

f: What does the author mean by saying Allah's speech is a meaning (maʿnā) established in His essence?
b: He means Allah's speech is an eternal inner reality belonging to Allah, not merely created expressions or physical sounds.

f: What does it mean that Allah's speech negates silence (sukūt)?
b: It means Allah's speech indicates that He is not one who refrains from speaking despite having the ability to speak.

f: What does it mean that Allah's speech negates incapacity (āfah)?
b: It means Allah is not prevented from speaking due to any inability or defect, unlike created beings whose inability may prevent speech.

f: What examples does the author give of human incapacity preventing speech?
b: He mentions natural inability such as being mute (al-kharas), and weakness of faculties such as in childhood.

f: How does the author answer the objection that silence and inability only apply to spoken words, not inner speech?
b: He says the intended meanings are inner silence and inner inability: not intending speech within oneself or lacking the ability to form such speech internally. Just as speech can be outward or inward, its opposite can also be outward or inward.

f: What does the author mean by saying Allah is "one who commands, forbids, and informs through it"?
b: He means Allah's one eternal attribute of speech has different manifestations according to its relationships: sometimes it relates to commands, sometimes prohibitions, and sometimes statements of information.

f: How can one eternal attribute have different types such as command and information?
b: The difference is not in the eternal attribute itself, but in its connections (taʿalluqat) and relations. This is similar to knowledge and power, which are one eternal attribute while their objects and relationships differ.

f: What distinction does the author make between the attribute itself and its تَعَلُّقَ (relation)?
b: The attribute remains eternal and one, while its تَعَلُّقَ to different things can vary and relate to created events.

f: Why do Ahl al-Sunnah say that Allah’s attributes are neither identical to His Essence nor other than His Essence?
b: They say this to avoid claiming that the attributes are separate eternal entities besides Allah, while also avoiding the claim that the attributes are merely the Essence itself. Thus the attributes are not “He” nor “other than Him” in the sense intended by theologians.

f: Why is saying that Allah’s attributes are completely identical to His Essence problematic?
b: Because if the attributes were identical to the Essence in every respect, then knowledge, power, life, and other attributes would all be the same thing without distinction, making knowledge, for example, also power and life.

f: How did some theologians explain the statement that Allah’s attributes are “neither He nor other than Him”?
b: They explained “other than Him” as meaning something whose existence can be conceived without the other. Allah’s attributes cannot exist independently from Him, so they are not “other” in this sense.

f: What objection is raised against defining “otherness” as the possibility of separation?
b: This definition would wrongly imply that many things known to be different are not different, such as the world and its Creator, or an accident and its subject, because one cannot exist without the other.

f: What problem occurs if “otherness” only requires separation from one side?
b: It would make the part not other than the whole and the attribute not other than the Essence, which contradicts ordinary understanding.

f: What is the weakness in the argument that one part of a whole is not other than the whole?
b: It is weak because the fact that something is included within a whole does not remove the distinction between the part and the complete entity.

f: What is meant by Allah’s eternal attributes?
b: They are attributes that have always existed with Allah and are not originated or created.

f: What is the definition of Allah’s attribute of knowledge?
b: Knowledge is an eternal attribute by which known things become manifest when Allah’s knowledge relates to them.

f: What is the definition of Allah’s attribute of power?
b: Power is an eternal attribute by which Allah brings about possible things when His power relates to them.

f: What is the definition of Allah’s attribute of life?
b: Life is an eternal attribute that necessitates the possibility of possessing knowledge.

f: What is meant by Allah’s attribute of strength (al-quwwah)?
b: It means power (al-qudrah).

f: What is Allah’s attribute of hearing?
b: Hearing is an eternal attribute through which Allah perceives all things that are heard.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of seeing?
b: Seeing is an eternal attribute through which Allah perceives all things that are seen with complete perception, without needing eyes, senses, air, or physical means.

f: Does the eternality of Allah’s hearing and seeing require that all heard and seen things are eternal?
b: No. The attributes are eternal, but their relationships to created things occur newly. Similarly, Allah’s eternal knowledge does not mean that all known things are eternal.

f: What are Allah’s will and choice (al-irādah and al-mashīʾah)?
b: They are an eternal attribute in the Living One that specifies one possible thing to occur at a particular time, even though Allah’s power relates equally to all possibilities.

f: What does Allah’s will not mean according to this explanation?
b: It does not mean that Allah is compelled, unaware, or overcome.

f: Why is Allah’s will not the same as command?
b: Because Allah commands people to believe and obey, but not everything He commands necessarily occurs. If command itself were identical to will, everything commanded would happen.

f: What is meant by Allah’s action and creation (al-fiʿl wa al-takhlīq)?
b: They refer to an eternal attribute called al-takwīn (bringing into existence).

f: Why does the author avoid using the word “creation” (khalq) when discussing the attribute?
b: Because “creation” is commonly used for the created thing itself, while the discussion concerns Allah’s eternal attribute.

f: What is the view of some theologians regarding creating, providing sustenance, giving life, and causing death?
b: They say these actions return to one eternal attribute in Allah called al-takwīn.

f: What is the Ashʿarī position mentioned regarding these actions?
b: The Ashʿarīs held that these are relations and attributes of actions rather than a separate eternal attribute of takwīn.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of speech (kalām)?
b: Speech is an eternal attribute existing with Allah’s Essence.

f: Why is Allah’s speech not the same as knowledge?
b: Because a person may speak about something he does not know, or may even state something he knows to be false.

f: Why is Allah’s speech not the same as will?
b: Because a person may command something without actually wanting it to occur, such as commanding someone to test whether they obey.

f: What is meant by “speech of the soul” (kalām nafsī)?
b: It is the inner meaning and intention present within oneself before it is expressed through words, writing, or signs.

f: What evidence does the author mention for the concept of inner speech?
b: He cites the statement of al-Akhṭal: “Indeed speech is in the heart; the tongue was only made as a sign of what is in the heart.”

f: What is the proof for affirming Allah’s attribute of speech?
b: The consensus of the Ummah and the continuous reports from the Prophets that Allah speaks, together with the impossibility of speech occurring without the attribute of speech.

f: How many eternal attributes does the author list for Allah?
b: Eight: knowledge, power, life, hearing, seeing, will, takwīn (creating), and speech.

f: Why does the author give special attention to will, takwīn, and speech?
b: Because these three attributes involve greater disagreement and subtle theological discussion.

f: Why does Allah being described as “Speaker” require Him to possess the attribute of speech?
b: Because a derived description requires the existence of the source from which it is derived. Someone cannot truly be called a speaker without speech.

f: Why is Allah’s speech not composed of letters and sounds?
b: Because letters and sounds are created accidents. Each sound depends on the ending of the previous one, and such succession cannot be eternal.

f: Which groups are refuted by saying Allah’s speech is not of the category of letters and sounds?
b: The Ḥanābilah and Karrāmiyyah who held that Allah’s speech consists of eternal letters and sounds.

f: What does it mean that Allah’s speech negates silence and defect?
b: It means Allah is not silent despite possessing the ability to speak, nor does He suffer any inability preventing speech.

f: How does the author answer the objection that silence only applies to spoken speech?
b: He says there is also inner silence and inner inability, just as there is inner speech and outward speech.

f: How can Allah’s one attribute of speech become commands, prohibitions, and reports?
b: The attribute itself remains one, but it becomes described differently according to its different relations and connections.

f: Why does the author say the multiplicity of Allah’s speech does not mean multiple attributes?
b: Because the difference occurs in the relations and objects of the attribute, not in the eternal attribute itself.

f: What is meant by the statement that the Qur’an is written in our manuscripts, preserved in our hearts, recited by our tongues, heard by our ears, yet not residing in them?
b: It means that the Qur’an, in its true reality, is the eternal meaning (kalām nafsī) قَائِمٌ (existing) in the Essence of Allah تَعَالَى. It is not physically contained in manuscripts, hearts, tongues, or ears. Rather, the written letters, spoken words, and sounds are expressions and indications of that eternal meaning.

f: How can the Qur’an be written, recited, heard, and memorized if it is not present in those things?
b: The answer is that things have different types of existence: existence in external reality (الْأَعْيَانُ), existence in the mind (الْأَذْهَانُ), existence in expression (الْعِبَارَةُ), and existence in writing (الْكِتَابَةُ). Writing indicates the spoken expression; spoken expression indicates the mental meaning; and the mental meaning corresponds to the external reality.

f: How does the author explain the difference between the eternal Qur’an and the created expressions of the Qur’an?
b: When the Qur’an is described with qualities belonging to eternal things, such as "the Qur’an is uncreated," the intended meaning is the eternal speech of Allah تَعَالَى. When it is described with qualities of created things, such as "I read half the Qur’an," "I memorized the Qur’an," or "a person in minor ritual impurity cannot touch the Qur’an," the intended meaning is the written, spoken, or imagined forms of the Qur’an.

f: Why did the scholars of Usul define the Qur’an as "that which is written in the manuscripts and transmitted through mass transmission"?
b: Because the evidence for legal rulings (aḥkām sharʿiyyah) depends upon the transmitted wording, not merely the eternal meaning. Therefore, they defined the Qur’an in relation to the wording and meaning together: the wording insofar as it indicates the meaning, not merely the meaning alone.

f: Can the eternal speech of Allah تَعَالَى itself be heard?
b: There was disagreement among scholars. Imam al-Ashʿarī held that it is possible for the eternal speech itself to be heard. Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāʾīnī and Shaykh Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī held that it cannot be heard directly; rather, what is heard is a sound that indicates Allah’s speech.

f: How is the verse "until he hears the speech of Allah" (التَّوْبَةُ: 6) understood according to those who deny directly hearing the eternal speech?
b: They explain that the person hears something indicating Allah’s speech, just as one says "I heard the knowledge of so-and-so," meaning he heard words conveying that knowledge. However, when Musa عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ heard Allah's speech without an intermediary of a book or angel, he was specifically called Kalīmullāh (the one who spoke directly with Allah).

f: If Allah’s speech refers truly to the eternal meaning, why is the spoken Qur’an also called the speech of Allah?
b: The author explains that "the speech of Allah" is a shared term referring to both the eternal speech (kalām nafsī) and the created expressions (the arranged letters and sounds). The attribution to Allah means that the wording was created by Allah and is not a composition of human beings.

f: Is the wording of the Qur’an considered merely metaphorically the speech of Allah?
b: The author says this needs clarification. The wording is not metaphorically attributed in the sense that it is unrelated to Allah. Rather, the true speech is the eternal meaning, and the wording is called speech because it indicates that meaning. Some scholars used the term "metaphor" only to indicate that the primary meaning of speech is the inner meaning.

f: What is the position of some later scholars regarding the meaning of "the speech of Allah"?
b: Some researchers explained that the "meaning" in "the speech of Allah is an eternal meaning" is not merely the concept understood from the wording, but something contrasted with physical entities. It means a non-independent attribute that does not stand by itself, like other attributes of Allah.

f: Why do the scholars reject the view of the Ḥanbalīs who claimed the arranged letters and wording of the Qur’an are eternal?
b: Because the arranged letters necessarily occur in sequence. For example, one cannot pronounce the letter س in "بِسْمِ اللَّهِ" before pronouncing the بِ. Anything whose parts depend on sequence and succession cannot be eternal.

f: What is meant by the statement: "The recited Qur’an is eternal, while the recitation is created"?
b: It means that the actual speech of Allah (the eternal meaning) has no sequence or division. However, when humans recite it, their pronunciation occurs through created sounds and letters that happen one after another due to the limitations of human speech organs.

f: How does the author explain the lack of sequence in Allah’s eternal speech?
b: Allah’s speech that exists in His Essence has no arrangement of parts or precedence of one part over another. The ordering only appears in human recitation because of the limitations of the tools of speech.

f: What do some scholars mean when they say that Allah’s speech has no sequence of parts?
b: They mean that Allah’s eternal speech (kalām nafsī) is not composed of ordered letters or sounds, because letters require sequence: one part must occur after another. Since Allah does not need speech organs, His speech is not arranged in this manner.

f: How do scholars explain the statement that a person’s internal speech is not composed of ordered parts?
b: They explain that when a person thinks of speech internally, the forms of letters are stored in his imagination. When he turns his attention to them, it becomes imagined words or written forms; when he pronounces them, it becomes audible speech. Allah’s speech, however, is not like this because it does not depend on imagination, organs, or sequence.

f: What is meant by the attribute of التَّكْوِينُ (formation/bringing into existence)?
b: التَّكْوِينُ is the meaning expressed by terms such as creating, making, producing, originating, and bringing into existence. It is explained as bringing something nonexistent out of nonexistence into existence.

f: Why is التَّكْوِينُ considered an eternal attribute of Allah according to those who affirm it?
b: Because reason and revelation agree that Allah is the Creator and Maker of the universe. It is impossible to apply the name "Creator" to something without the attribute from which the name is derived being established for it. Therefore, التَّكْوِينُ must be eternal.

f: What is the first proof that التَّكْوِينُ is eternal?
b: It is impossible for newly originated attributes (ḥawādith) to occur within Allah’s Essence, because this would make Allah a place where events occur, which is impossible.

f: What is the second proof that التَّكْوِينُ is eternal?
b: Allah described Himself in His eternal speech as the Creator. If He was not eternally the Creator, this would require either falsehood, metaphorical usage without necessity, or that He only becomes Creator in the future. Since He truly is the Creator, His attribute of creation must be eternal.

f: What is the third proof that التَّكْوِينُ is eternal?
b: If التَّكْوِينُ were created, it would either come into existence through another act of التَّكْوِينُ, leading to an infinite regress, or it would occur without a creator, meaning a created thing exists without a cause. Both are impossible.

f: What is the fourth proof that التَّكْوِينُ is eternal?
b: If التَّكْوِينُ were created, it would either occur in Allah’s Essence, making Him subject to created events, or occur in something else. The latter would imply that another thing becomes the creator, which is also impossible.

f: What assumption are these proofs based upon?
b: These proofs are based upon the view that التَّكْوِينُ is a real eternal attribute, similar to knowledge and power.

f: What is the position of the more precise theologians regarding التَّكْوِينُ?
b: Many theologians hold that التَّكْوِينُ is not an independent real attribute, but rather a rational relation and consideration (iḍāfah/itibār ʿaqlī), similar to descriptions such as Allah being before everything, with everything, after everything, worshipped by creation, and the One who gives life and death.

f: According to those who deny that التَّكْوِينُ is a separate attribute, what exists eternally?
b: They say that what exists eternally is the source of creating, providing, giving life, and causing death. There is no proof that التَّكْوِينُ itself is an additional attribute besides Allah’s power and will.

f: How do they explain creation without affirming a separate attribute of التَّكْوِينُ?
b: They explain that Allah’s power alone does not determine one possibility over another, but when combined with His eternal will, one possibility becomes specified. Thus creation occurs through the combination of power and will.

f: What argument do those who say التَّكْوِينُ is created use?
b: They argue that التَّكْوِينُ cannot exist without the thing being created, just as striking cannot exist without something struck. If التَّكْوِينُ were eternal, then its objects of creation would also have to be eternal, which is impossible.

f: How does the author respond to the argument that التَّكْوِينُ requires the created object to exist eternally?
b: He responds that التَّكْوِينُ itself is eternal, but its connection to created things occurs at the time Allah wills them to exist according to His knowledge and will. Just as Allah’s knowledge and power are eternal but their connections to created things occur when those things come into existence.

f: Does the eternity of an attribute require the eternity of its objects?
b: No. Eternal attributes such as Allah’s knowledge and power do not require eternal objects. Their relationships (taʿalluqāt) with created things occur when those things come into existence.

f: What does it mean that Allah’s التَّكْوِينُ is eternal but the created thing is not eternal?
b: It means that Allah’s attribute remains eternally existing, while the created thing comes into existence at the specific time determined by Allah’s knowledge and will.

f: How does the author respond to the claim that something dependent on another thing must be created?
b: He says this argument relies on the philosophers’ definition of eternal and created things. According to philosophers, anything dependent on another is "created in essence." However, according to theologians, something created is what has a beginning and was preceded by nonexistence. Mere dependence does not necessarily mean temporal origination.

f: Why does dependence on Allah not necessarily imply temporal beginning?
b: Because something could depend on another eternally, continuously receiving existence from it. This is the view attributed to philosophers regarding some things they considered eternally dependent, such as the prime matter (hayūlā).

f: What condition does the author mention under which saying that the world’s existence depends on Allah’s التَّكْوِينُ would imply that the world is created?
b: If it is established that the world proceeds from Allah through choice and will (ikhtiyār), rather than through necessary emanation (ījāb), by a proof that does not depend on the world being created, then saying that the world depends on Allah’s التَّكْوِينُ would imply that it is created.

f: Why does the author mention that Allah’s التَّكْوِينُ applies to every part of the world?
b: He mentions this to refute those who claimed that some parts of the world, such as the prime matter (al-hayūlā), are eternal. Those philosophers only claimed its eternity in the sense that it was not preceded by nonexistence, not that it was independent of Allah’s creation.

f: Do theologians accept that التَّكْوِينُ cannot exist without the created thing (الْمُكَوَّنُ)?
b: No. They reject the idea that التَّكْوِينُ must exist together with the created thing. They argue that التَّكْوِينُ is not like striking, which requires both the striker and the thing struck.

f: What is the difference between striking and التَّكْوِينُ?
b: Striking is a relational attribute (ṣifah iḍāfiyyah) that cannot be imagined without both sides of the relation: the striker and the thing struck. However, التَّكْوِينُ is a real attribute (ṣifah ḥaqīqiyyah) that is the source of the relation of bringing something from nonexistence into existence.

f: Why does the author reject comparing التَّكْوِينُ to striking?
b: Because striking is an accident that cannot remain, so its effect and relation require the object struck to exist simultaneously. Allah’s act of creating, however, is eternal and necessarily enduring, remaining until the time when the created thing comes into existence.

f: What is the position of the theologians regarding التَّكْوِينُ and the created thing?
b: They hold that التَّكْوِينُ is different from the created thing (الْمُكَوَّنُ). The act of creating is not identical with the thing created.

f: What proof is given that التَّكْوِينُ is not identical with the created thing?
b: The author argues that an action is necessarily different from its object, like striking is different from the thing struck and eating is different from the thing eaten.

f: What would be the consequence if التَّكْوِينُ were identical with the created thing?
b: It would mean that the created thing creates itself, because the created thing would be the same as the التَّكْوِينُ through which it was created. This would make it eternal and independent of the Creator, which is impossible.

f: What other problem results from saying التَّكْوِينُ is identical with the created thing?
b: It would mean that Allah’s only relationship to the world is that He existed before it and had power over it, without actually creating or influencing it. This would not truly make Him the Creator of the world.

f: Why would saying التَّكْوِينُ is identical with the created thing deny Allah being the Creator?
b: Because a creator is one who performs the act of creation, and the created thing would instead be the act itself. There would be no separate act of creation attributed to Allah.

f: What conclusion does the author draw about Allah’s relationship to creation?
b: Allah تَعَالَى is the One who creates and forms things, while the created things are His creations. The act of creation is an attribute belonging to Allah, not identical with the created objects.

f: Why does the author say that Allah cannot be described as the created thing?
b: Because the term "created" (مُكَوَّنُ) refers to something upon which التَّكْوِينِ occurs, while التَّكْوِينُ is an attribute belonging to the Creator. They are distinct realities.

f: What example does the author give to show the absurdity of confusing the creator and the created?
b: He says it would be like saying the Creator of the blackness in a stone is black, or that the stone itself creates the blackness. This is incorrect because the attribute belongs to the one in whom the relevant quality exists.

f: Why does the author warn against taking the statement "التَّكْوِينُ is different from the created thing" in an obviously impossible way?
b: Because it would be unreasonable to attribute an obviously false belief to the great scholars of Usul. Rather, their words should be understood in a way that allows a valid scholarly disagreement.

f: What do scholars mean when they say "التَّكْوِينُ is not the created thing"?
b: They mean that when a doer performs an action, there are only two realities: the doer and the object acted upon. The "creation" or "bringing into existence" (التَّكْوِينُ وَالْإِيجَادُ) is a rational relation understood from connecting the doer to the created object; it is not necessarily an independently existing thing in external reality.

f: What do scholars not mean when they say التَّكْوِينُ is not the created thing?
b: They do not mean that the concept of التَّكْوِينُ is exactly identical to the concept of the created object, because that would lead to impossible conclusions.

f: What analogy does the author give to explain the relationship between التَّكْوِينُ and the created thing?
b: He compares it to the debate about whether existence (الْوُجُودُ) is identical with essence (الْمَاهِيَّةُ) externally. The essence does not have a separate existence apart from the existence attached to it, yet the mind can distinguish between the two concepts.

f: How does the author explain the relationship between essence and existence?
b: He explains that externally, a thing’s essence and its existence are not two separate realities like a body and its color. Rather, when an essence exists, its existence is its actualization. However, the mind can consider essence separately from existence and vice versa.

f: What would be required to refute the view that التَّكْوِينُ is not a separate attribute?
b: One would need to prove that Allah’s bringing things into existence depends upon a real attribute قَائِم بِذَاتِهِ (existing in His Essence) that is separate from His power and will.

f: What is the more precise explanation of التَّكْوِينُ according to the author?
b: When Allah’s power is connected to the existence of something at the time He wills it to exist, this relation is called "bringing into existence" (ījād) when attributed to the power, and "creation/takwīn" when attributed to Allah as the Creator.

f: According to this explanation, what is the reality of creation?
b: Its reality is that Allah’s Essence is such that His power is connected to bringing the thing into existence at its appointed time. Then, according to the specific created things, different names apply, such as providing, shaping, giving life, and causing death.

f: Are providing, shaping, giving life, and causing death separate eternal attributes according to the author?
b: No. They all return to the single concept of التَّكْوِينُ. The difference comes from the different objects and relationships of the attribute.

f: What view does the author say some scholars of Transoxiana held regarding these acts?
b: Some held that each of these acts is a separate eternal real attribute. The author says this view greatly multiplies the number of eternal attributes, even if they are not considered completely separate from each other.

f: What view does the author consider closer to the truth?
b: The view of the researchers among the theologians: that all these acts return to التَّكْوِينُ, and their differences are due only to different relationships and objects.

f: How does التَّكْوِينُ relate to different acts of Allah?
b: When related to life, it is called giving life (iḥyāʾ); when related to death, it is called causing death (imātah); when related to form, it is called shaping (taṣwīr); when related to provision, it is called providing (tarzīq). All of these are forms of التَّكْوِينُ.

f: Why does the author repeat that التَّكْوِينُ is an eternal attribute established in Allah’s Essence?
b: He repeats it for emphasis and clarification, not merely to prove that Allah has an additional ancient attribute.

f: What does Allah’s eternal will mean according to the author?
b: It is an eternal attribute of Allah that specifies things: choosing one possibility over another and determining that something occurs at one time rather than another.

f: What groups does the author mention as holding incorrect views about Allah’s will?
b: He mentions the philosophers, who claimed Allah acts by necessity rather than choice; the Najjāriyyah, who said Allah wills by His Essence rather than by an attribute; some Muʿtazilah, who claimed His will is created but not in a place; and the Karrāmiyyah, who said His will is created within His Essence.

f: What evidence does the author give that Allah has an eternal attribute of will?
b: He cites Qur’anic verses affirming Allah’s will and desire, the impossibility of created events existing within Allah’s Essence, and the order and perfection of the universe as evidence that its Creator acts with choice and will.

f: How does the existence and order of the universe prove Allah acts by will?
b: The universe’s existence in such a precise and beneficial arrangement indicates that its Creator is a choosing and powerful agent, not merely a necessary cause.

f: How does the occurrence of the universe prove Allah is not a necessary cause like the philosophers claimed?
b: If Allah created by necessity of His Essence, then the effect would have to be eternal along with the cause, because a necessary cause cannot fail to produce its effect. Since the universe is originated, Allah must act by choice.

f: What is meant by "the vision of Allah" (رُؤْيَةُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى)?
b: It means complete perception through sight: perceiving something as it truly is, just as seeing the full moon gives a more complete disclosure than merely knowing it exists without looking at it.

f: Is seeing Allah rationally possible according to the author?
b: Yes. The author says it is permissible in reason (جَائِزَةٌ فِي الْعَقْلِ), meaning the intellect by itself does not judge it impossible unless there is evidence proving impossibility.

f: What proof do the people of truth give for the possibility of seeing Allah?
b: They give both a rational proof and a textual proof.

f: What is the first rational argument for the possibility of seeing Allah?
b: Humans can see bodies and accidents. Anything that shares a common ruling must have a common basis. The possible causes are existence, origination, or possibility. Since nonexistence cannot be the cause, existence remains. Allah and created things both share existence, so seeing is not impossible for Allah merely because He exists differently from creation.

f: Why does the ability to see created things prove that seeing Allah is not impossible?
b: Because the basis for vision is existence itself, not necessarily being a body or accident. Therefore, if existence is the cause that allows vision, Allah’s existence also does not prevent vision.

f: Why are sounds, tastes, and smells not normally seen despite existing?
b: According to the author, this is not because seeing them is rationally impossible, but because Allah did not create the normal habit (ʿādah) of humans seeing them.

f: How does the author answer the objection that the possibility of vision does not need a cause?
b: He says that the intended "cause" is the object of vision and its suitability for being perceived. The object must be something existing, not merely an absence.

f: Why does the author argue that the object of vision is not specifically a body or accident?
b: Because when we first see something from far away, we only perceive its identity or existence, not whether it is a substance, accident, human, or horse. The details come later.

f: What is the textual proof for the possibility of seeing Allah?
b: The author cites Musa عليه السلام asking Allah: {رَبِّ أَرِنِي أَنْظُرْ إِلَيْكَ} ("My Lord, show me, that I may look at You").

f: Why does Musa’s عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ request for vision prove its possibility?
b: Because if seeing Allah were impossible, Musa’s عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ request would have been ignorance, foolishness, and asking for something impossible. Prophets are protected from such things.

f: How does the author explain Allah making the vision dependent on the stability of the mountain?
b: Allah connected the vision to the mountain remaining stable. Since the condition itself was possible, the thing dependent upon it is also possible. Something impossible cannot become possible under any circumstance.

f: Why do the Ashʿarīs reject the idea that Allah’s attributes are completely identical to His Essence?
b: Because if the attributes were identical to the Essence in every sense, then knowledge, power, life, etc. would all be the same thing in meaning. This would require knowledge itself to be power, life, knowledgeable, living, powerful, and the creator of the world, which is impossible.

f: What is the Ashʿarī position regarding Allah’s attributes in relation to His Essence?
b: Allah’s attributes are neither identical to His Essence nor completely other than it. They are not separate entities, so this does not imply multiple eternal beings, but they are also not simply the Essence itself.

f: Why did the Muʿtazilah deny additional eternal attributes of Allah?
b: They argued that affirming eternal attributes distinct from Allah’s Essence would imply multiple eternal beings and contradict tawḥīd.

f: How do the Ashʿarīs answer the argument that affirming attributes creates multiple eternals?
b: They say the impossibility is only in having multiple eternal essences, not in having one eternal Essence with attributes. Allah’s Essence is eternal, and His attributes are eternal by Him, not independent eternal beings.

f: Why should one not say simply that Allah and His attributes are “eternal beings”?
b: Because this wording may suggest that the attributes are independent entities possessing divinity. Rather, Allah alone is the Necessary Being in Himself, while His attributes are necessary through Him.

f: What does it mean that Allah’s attributes are “not Him and not other than Him”?
b: It means they are not identical with the Essence in concept, nor are they separate beings existing independently. There is an intermediate relationship like the relationship between a quality and its possessor.

f: What objection is raised against saying that Allah’s attributes are neither identical nor other?
b: The objection is that denying otherness seems to imply identity, and denying identity seems to imply otherness, leaving no middle position.

f: How do scholars answer the objection that there is no middle between identity and otherness?
b: They define “otherness” as two things being capable of existing separately. Allah’s Essence and attributes cannot be separated, but their concepts are distinct. Therefore, they are neither identical nor separate.

f: Why is the comparison between Allah’s attributes and created attributes not exact?
b: Created attributes can be separated from their subjects in concept and sometimes in existence, whereas Allah’s eternal attributes are inseparable from His Essence.

f: What are the eternal attributes of Allah mentioned here?
b: Knowledge (الْعِلْمُ), power (الْقُدْرَةُ), life (الْحَيَاةُ), strength (الْقُوَّةُ), hearing (السَّمْعُ), sight (الْبَصَرُ), will/desire (الْإِرَادَةُ وَالْمَشِيئَةُ), action/creating (الْفِعْلُ وَالتَّخْلِيقُ or التَّكْوِينُ), and speech (الْكَلَامُ).

f: What is Allah’s attribute of knowledge?
b: It is an eternal attribute by which all things become known when He relates it to them.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of power?
b: It is an eternal attribute by which Allah brings possibilities into existence when His power relates to them.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of life?
b: It is an eternal attribute that makes knowledge possible.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of hearing?
b: It is an eternal attribute related to all things heard.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of sight?
b: It is an eternal attribute related to all things seen, allowing complete perception without imagination, assumption, physical senses, or receiving light.

f: Does the eternity of Allah’s hearing and sight require the eternity of things heard and seen?
b: No. Just as Allah’s eternal knowledge and power do not require eternal known things or created things, His hearing and sight do not require eternal objects of hearing and seeing.

f: What are Allah’s will (irādah) and will/desire (mashīʾah)?
b: They are expressions for an attribute in the living Being that specifies one possibility among many possible things at a particular time, despite Allah’s power relating equally to all possibilities.

f: What is the difference between Allah’s knowledge and His will regarding events?
b: Allah’s knowledge follows what occurs in the sense that He knows things as they are, while His will specifies which possible event occurs.

f: What does the author say against those who claim Allah’s will is not an eternal attribute?
b: He rejects the claim that Allah’s will is either created in His Essence or merely identical with His Essence, because revelation affirms Allah’s will and it is impossible for created things to exist in Allah’s Essence.

f: What is meant by Allah’s action and creation (الْفِعْلُ وَالتَّخْلِيقُ)?
b: It refers to the eternal attribute called “takwīn” (bringing into existence), through which creation, producing, originating, and causing things to exist occur.

f: Why does the author avoid using only the word “creation” (خَلَقَ) for this attribute?
b: Because “creation” is commonly used for the created thing itself, whereas he wants to refer to the eternal divine attribute.

f: What is “takwīn” (التَّكْوِينُ)?
b: It is the meaning expressed by actions such as creating, producing, originating, making, and bringing from non-existence into existence.

f: Why do some scholars say takwīn is an eternal attribute of Allah?
b: Because Allah is described as Creator in revelation. If He were not eternally Creator, describing Him as such would either be false or metaphorical without necessity.

f: What argument is given that takwīn cannot be created?
b: If takwīn were created, it would either require another takwīn to create it, causing infinite regress, or exist without a creator, which is impossible.

f: What is the view of many later theologians regarding takwīn?
b: They considered takwīn not a separate real eternal attribute but a rational relation connected to Allah’s power and will, like saying Allah is Creator, Giver of life, and Provider.

f: How do scholars who affirm eternal takwīn respond to the claim that creation requires the created thing to exist?
b: They say takwīn is not identical to the created thing. It is an eternal attribute whose relation to created things occurs when they come into existence, just like knowledge and power have eternal existence but changing relations.

f: Is Allah’s act of creating identical with the created object?
b: No. The act and the object created are distinct. Otherwise, the created thing would create itself and be independent of Allah.

f: Why must Allah’s action be different from His created things?
b: Because if the action were identical to the created thing, there would be no real Creator-creation relationship and created things would exist by themselves.

f: What clarification does the author give regarding “takwīn is not the created thing”?
b: He explains that scholars mean the act of bringing something into existence is not the same as the thing brought into existence; they do not mean that there is necessarily a separate physical entity called “takwīn.”

f: What is the conclusion regarding takwīn according to the strongest view mentioned?
b: The closest view is that all specific acts (giving life, causing death, providing, shaping, etc.) return to the single concept of takwīn, while their differences come from their different relations.

f: What is Allah’s will described as in relation to His Essence?
b: It is an eternal attribute existing in Allah’s Essence, which specifies things according to His wisdom and choice.

f: What is the Ashʿarī proof that Allah acts by choice rather than necessity?
b: The ordered existence of the universe indicates a wise, choosing Creator. If Allah acted necessarily by His Essence, the universe would have had to exist eternally with Him.

f: What is meant by the possibility of seeing Allah (ruʾyat Allāh)?
b: It means that reason alone does not judge the vision of Allah to be impossible unless there is proof preventing it.

f: What is the Ashʿarī rational proof for the possibility of seeing Allah?
b: Created things are seen because they exist. Existence is the common factor between all things seen. Since Allah exists, there is no rational proof that His existence prevents vision.

f: Why does the fact that created bodies are seen not mean Allah must be a body?
b: Because being seen is not necessarily dependent on being a body; the common factor is existence, not physicality.

f: What is the Qur’anic proof for the believers seeing Allah?
b: The verse: {وُجُوْهٌ يّوْمَئِذٍ نَاضِرَةٌ ۝ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ} (Qiyāmah 75:22–23).

f: What is the hadith evidence for seeing Allah?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “Indeed, you will see your Lord as you see the moon on the night of the full moon.”

f: What is the ijmāʿ evidence for seeing Allah?
b: The early Muslim community agreed that believers will see Allah in the Hereafter before opposing interpretations appeared.

f: What is the main rational objection against seeing Allah?
b: Opponents argue that vision requires the object to be in a place, direction, facing the observer, at a distance, and reached by a physical ray from the eye—all of which cannot apply to Allah.

f: How do Ashʿarīs answer the objection that vision requires direction and distance?
b: They reject that such conditions are necessary for vision itself. Those conditions only apply to ordinary created vision, not necessarily to Allah’s vision.

f: Why can’t Allah’s vision be compared completely to created vision?
b: Because Allah is not a physical object, and applying the rules of physical perception to Him is comparing the unseen to the seen.

f: What objection is made against the possibility of seeing Allah if all conditions of vision are present?
b: The objection says that if vision is possible whenever its conditions exist, then Allah would necessarily be seen whenever those conditions exist. Otherwise, it would be possible for huge mountains to be present before us while we do not see them, which would be absurd.

f: How do the scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah answer the claim that vision must occur whenever its conditions exist?
b: They reject that vision necessarily follows from the physical conditions alone. Allah creates vision in the observer, and He may choose not to create it even when the apparent conditions exist.

f: What Qur’anic verse is used by opponents to deny the vision of Allah?
b: The verse: {لَا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصَارُ وَهُوَ يُدْرِكُ الْأَبْصَارَ} (Al-Anʿām 6:103).

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah respond to the verse {لَا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصَارُ}?
b: They say it does not prove the impossibility of seeing Allah unless one accepts that “al-idrāk” means vision in every sense and that the verse means absolute negation at all times and in all circumstances.

f: How can the verse {لَا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصَارُ} actually indicate the possibility of seeing Allah?
b: If Allah could never be seen, there would be no praise in saying He is not seen, just as an absent or nonexistent thing is not praised for being unseen. The praise indicates that He could be seen but is not fully encompassed.

f: What is meant if “idrāk” is interpreted as complete encompassing vision?
b: The meaning would be that Allah can be seen but cannot be encompassed by sight because He is beyond limits, boundaries, and dimensions.

f: How do scholars answer the verses where the request to see Allah is treated with rejection?
b: They say the rejection was because of the stubbornness and arrogance of the people asking, not because seeing Allah is impossible.

f: What evidence shows that seeing Allah in this world was considered possible by some?
b: The disagreement among the Companions regarding whether the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah on the Night Journey indicates that they considered the matter possible, even if they differed about whether it occurred.

f: What is the view regarding seeing Allah in dreams?
b: Many early scholars reported that it occurs. It is a type of witnessing through the heart, not through physical eyesight.

f: What is the belief of Ahl al-Sunnah regarding the actions of servants?
b: Allah is the Creator of all actions of His servants, including disbelief, faith, obedience, and sin.

f: What did the Muʿtazilah claim regarding human actions?
b: They claimed that humans create their own actions independently.

f: Why did some early Muʿtazilah avoid calling humans “creators”?
