b: They avoided the term because “creator” implies bringing something from nonexistence into existence, which they initially reserved for Allah.

f: Why did later Muʿtazilah use the term “creator” for humans?
b: They argued that terms like “creator,” “originator,” and “producer” all have the same meaning, so they permitted using “creator” for human actions.

f: What is the first rational proof that humans do not create their own actions?
b: If humans truly created their actions by power and choice, they would know every detail of those actions, because intentional creation requires complete knowledge of what is created.

f: Why does human experience contradict the idea that humans create their own actions?
b: A person walking does not know all the details of his movements, such as every intermediate stillness and variation in speed, nor the movements of muscles and nerves involved.

f: Why is ignorance of bodily movements significant in this argument?
b: Because walking is among the clearest voluntary human actions, yet humans are unaware of many details within it. Therefore, they cannot be the true creators of those actions.

f: What Qur’anic verse is used as evidence that Allah creates human actions?
b: {وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ} — “Allah created you and what you do.” (Al-Ṣāffāt 37:96).

f: How is the verse {وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ} interpreted?
b: “Mā taʿmalūn” can mean either “what you do” (the actions themselves) or “your works.” In either case, it indicates that Allah is the Creator of human actions.

f: Why does the proof not depend only on interpreting “mā” as a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah)?
b: Because even if “mā” is taken as a relative pronoun meaning “what you do,” the created things intended are the actual movements and actions resulting from human activity.

f: What distinction is made between an action and the creation of an action?
b: The “action” in terms of human attribution refers to the movement or deed that occurs, while creation refers to bringing that action into existence. Allah creates the existence of the act, while the servant performs it.

f: What other Qur’anic verse supports Allah being the Creator of everything?
b: {اللَّهُ خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ} — “Allah is the Creator of everything.” (Al-Zumar 39:62).

f: How does the verse {اللَّهُ خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ} support this doctrine?
b: Since human actions are things that exist and are possible, they fall under Allah’s general creation of all things.

f: What verse is mentioned regarding the difference between the Creator and creation?
b: {أَفَمَنْ يَخْلُقُ كَمَنْ لَا يَخْلُقُ} — “Is the One who creates like one who does not create?” (Al-Naḥl 16:17).

f: Why does the ability to create establish deserving of worship?
b: Because creating and bringing things into existence is a unique divine attribute and therefore a reason for deserving worship.

f: Why did some scholars reject the idea that Allah's attributes are other than His Essence?
b: Because they feared that affirming attributes additional to Allah’s Essence would imply multiple eternal entities, which they considered a negation of tawḥīd. They argued that Allah’s attributes are identical with His Essence, meaning His Essence is called “Knowing” due to its relation to known things, “Powerful” due to its relation to possible things, and so on.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah respond to the claim that affirming eternal attributes necessitates multiple eternals?
b: They respond that what is impossible is multiple eternal essences, not an eternal Essence with eternal attributes. The attributes are neither identical to the Essence nor separate entities from it; rather, they are attributes subsisting in Allah’s Essence.

f: What problem results from saying Allah’s attributes are identical to His Essence?
b: It would require that knowledge itself be power, life, the Knower, the Powerful, and the Creator, and would lead to many contradictions.

f: What was the position of the Karrāmiyyah regarding Allah’s attributes?
b: They affirmed Allah’s attributes but claimed they are originated (ḥādith), because they considered it impossible for originated things to subsist in Allah’s Essence.

f: Why do the Ashʿarīs say Allah’s attributes are neither He nor other than Him?
b: Because Allah’s attributes are not identical with His Essence, nor are they separate entities existing independently from Him. This avoids both denying the attributes and claiming multiple eternal beings.

f: Why did Christians fall into the problem of multiple eternals according to this discussion?
b: Because they affirmed three distinct hypostases (aqānīm): existence, knowledge, and life, which they called the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Since they allowed separation and transfer (such as the hypostasis of knowledge entering the body of Jesus عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ), they treated them as distinct entities.

f: How is the objection that “neither He nor other than Him” contradicts logic answered?
b: The Ashʿarīs explain that “otherness” means the possibility of separation and independent existence, while “identity” means complete unity of concept. A thing can be neither identical nor separate, such as a part in relation to a whole or an attribute in relation to its subject.

f: Why cannot Allah’s attributes be compared to ordinary parts and wholes?
b: Because the relationship between Allah’s Essence and His attributes is unique. Attributes are not independent parts like physical components, nor are they separate entities.

f: What are Allah’s eternal attributes mentioned here?
b: They are: knowledge (ʿilm), power (qudrah), life (ḥayāh), strength (quwwah), hearing (samʿ), seeing (baṣar), will (irādah/mashīʾah), creating/forming (takwīn), and speech (kalām).

f: What is Allah’s attribute of knowledge?
b: It is an eternal attribute by which all knowable things become manifest when related to it.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of power?
b: It is an eternal attribute by which possible things are brought into existence when related to them.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of life?
b: It is an eternal attribute that necessitates the possibility of knowledge.

f: What is meant by Allah’s attribute of strength (quwwah)?
b: It means power (qudrah).

f: What is Allah’s attribute of hearing?
b: It is an eternal attribute connected to all things that can be heard.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of seeing?
b: It is an eternal attribute connected to all visible things, perceiving them completely, not through imagination, illusion, bodily senses, or physical processes.

f: Does the eternality of Allah’s hearing and seeing require that all heard and seen things are eternal?
b: No. Just as Allah’s eternal knowledge does not require eternal known things, His eternal hearing and seeing do not require eternal objects of hearing and sight. The relations (taʿalluqs) occur with created things.

f: What are Allah’s will (irādah) and volition (mashīʾah)?
b: They are expressions for an attribute in the Living One that specifies one possible thing to occur at a particular time, despite Allah’s power being equally related to all possibilities.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah refute those who say Allah’s will means only that He is not forced, forgetful, or overcome?
b: They say this definition is insufficient because Allah’s will regarding His own actions and the actions of others is established by revelation. If His will only meant lack of compulsion, then it would not explain why some things occur rather than others.

f: What is the attribute of action and creation (fiʿl and takhwīn)?
b: It refers to Allah’s eternal attribute called takwīn, through which creation, bringing into existence, originating, and forming are expressed.

f: Why is the term “creation” avoided in describing the eternal attribute?
b: Because “creation” is commonly used for the created object itself, whereas the discussion concerns Allah’s eternal attribute.

f: What is meant by Allah’s provision (tarzīq)?
b: It is a specific manifestation of the attribute of takwīn, just as creating, shaping, giving life, and causing death are specific manifestations of it.

f: What is the Ashʿarī view of takwīn?
b: The Ashʿarīs generally considered takwīn not an additional real eternal attribute, but rather relations and considerations connected to Allah’s actions.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of speech (kalām)?
b: It is an eternal attribute expressed by the term “speech,” and it is a meaning subsisting in Allah’s Essence, not created letters and sounds.

f: Why is Allah’s speech not the same as knowledge or will?
b: Because a person may speak about something he does not know or may command something he does not want to happen, such as commanding someone as a test.

f: What is “kalām nafsī” (inner speech)?
b: It is the meaning existing within oneself before it is expressed through speech, writing, or signs.

f: What evidence is given for Allah being described as speaking?
b: The consensus of the Ummah and the continuous transmission from the prophets that Allah is a speaker. It is impossible to attribute speech to someone without affirming a real attribute of speech.

f: Why do Ashʿarīs reject the idea that Allah’s speech is composed of letters and sounds?
b: Because letters and sounds are created accidents that occur sequentially; one letter depends on the ending of another. Such temporal occurrences cannot subsist eternally in Allah’s Essence.

f: What is the Ashʿarī position regarding the Qur’an being uncreated?
b: The Qur’an is the speech of Allah and is uncreated in its true reality, meaning the eternal divine speech. The written letters, sounds, and recitations are created expressions that indicate that eternal speech.

f: Why do scholars say “the Qur’an is the speech of Allah, uncreated” rather than simply “the Qur’an is uncreated”?
b: To prevent misunderstanding that the physical letters, sounds, and written forms are themselves eternal, which was the view attributed to some Ḥanbalīs.

f: How do Ashʿarīs answer the objection that the Qur’an is written, recited, and heard, therefore created?
b: They distinguish between different levels of existence: the reality in itself, the mental representation, verbal expression, and written form. The eternal meaning is Allah’s speech, while the written and spoken forms are created indicators of it.

f: Can Allah’s eternal speech be heard directly?
b: Ashʿarī scholars differed. Al-Ashʿarī allowed that it may be heard, while Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāʾīnī denied this and said what is heard is something indicating Allah’s speech, like a voice created for that purpose.

f: Why is Moses عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ called “the one spoken to” (kalīm Allāh)?
b: Because Moses عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ heard a created sound without an intermediary of a book or angel that indicated Allah’s eternal speech.

f: What is the difference between eternal speech and the written Qur’an?
b: Eternal speech is the divine meaning subsisting in Allah’s Essence. The written Qur’an is composed of letters and forms created to indicate that speech.

f: What is meant by “the recited Qur’an is ancient, but the recitation is created”?
b: The meaning being conveyed is eternal, while the human act of reading and the sounds produced are created.

f: What is Allah’s attribute of takwīn according to those who affirm it as eternal?
b: It is an eternal attribute by which Allah brings things from non-existence into existence.

f: What arguments are given for the eternality of takwīn?
b: It is argued that Allah describes Himself as Creator eternally; originated attributes cannot subsist in Allah’s Essence; and if takwīn were originated it would either require another takwīn (leading to infinite regress) or exist without a cause.

f: What is the objection of scholars who deny takwīn as a separate eternal attribute?
b: They argue that takwīn is not a separate real attribute but an intellectual relation, like saying Allah is Creator, Provider, Giver of life, or Causer of death. These are different relations of His eternal power and will.

f: How do they answer the argument that takwīn requires a created object?
b: They say takwīn remains eternal, while its connection to created things occurs when those things come into existence. This is like Allah’s knowledge and power being eternal without requiring eternal objects.

f: Why is takwīn different from striking (ḍarb) and other created actions?
b: Striking is a relational action that requires both striker and struck object, while takwīn is considered a real divine attribute from which the relation of creating arises.

f: Why do they say Allah’s takwīn is not identical to the created thing?
b: Because if creation itself were identical with takwīn, the created thing would be creating itself, making it independent of Allah, which is impossible.

f: What is the meaning of “Allah’s will is eternal and subsisting in His Essence”?
b: It means Allah eternally specifies which possible things occur, at which times, without being compelled or changing in His Essence.

f: What is the Islamic position regarding seeing Allah in the Hereafter?
b: It is obligatory based on transmitted evidence. The believers will see Allah in the Hereafter.

f: What Qur’anic verse is used as evidence for believers seeing Allah?
b: {وُجُوْهٌ يّوْمَئِذٍ نَاضِرَةٌ ۝ إِلَى رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ} (Qur’an 75:22–23).

f: What hadith is used as evidence for seeing Allah?
b: “Indeed, you will see your Lord as you see the moon on the night of the full moon.”

f: What is the rational argument for the possibility of seeing Allah?
b: Everything existing can potentially be seen because the common factor between visible things is existence. Since Allah exists, seeing Him is not rationally impossible unless there is proof preventing it.

f: What is the response to the claim that seeing requires location, direction, and distance?
b: The requirement of place, direction, and physical connection applies only to created things. Allah’s seeing is unlike created seeing and does not require these conditions.

f: How is the verse {لَا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصَارُ} (“Eyes cannot perceive Him”) answered?
b: It does not deny seeing Allah, but rather complete encompassing perception. Allah can be seen without being encompassed by human sight.

f: Why did Allah reject the demand of those who asked Musa عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ to see Him?
b: Their request was out of stubbornness and challenge, not because seeing Allah is impossible.

f: What is the position of the scholars regarding seeing Allah in a dream?
b: Many early scholars transmitted that it can occur. It is a type of witnessing by the heart, not physical sight by the eyes.

f: What is the belief of Ahl al-Sunnah regarding human actions?
b: Allah is the Creator of all actions of servants, including disbelief, faith, obedience, and disobedience.

f: What was the Muʿtazilah position regarding human actions?
b: They claimed humans are the creators of their own actions.

f: What is the first rational argument against the Muʿtazilah position?
b: If humans created their own actions, they would know all details of them. Yet humans are unaware of many details of their movements, such as the precise motions of muscles and limbs involved in walking.

f: What Qur’anic evidence is used to show Allah creates human actions?
b: {وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ} — “Allah created you and what you do.” (Qur’an 37:96)

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah explain the verse “Allah created you and what you do”?
b: They say it refers to the actions themselves (the things produced by actions), not necessarily the human choice and intention.

f: Why does Allah being the Creator of actions not mean humans have no responsibility?
b: Because Ahl al-Sunnah affirm human choice and acquisition (kasb). Divine creation of actions does not negate human intention, choice, praise, blame, reward, and punishment.

f: How do the Muʿtazilah argue against Allah creating human actions?
b: They argue that people clearly distinguish voluntary movement from involuntary trembling, and that if Allah created all actions, accountability and moral responsibility would become meaningless.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah respond to the argument that Allah creating sins means He is the sinner?
b: They explain that the one who performs an action is the one in whom the action subsists, not the one who creates it. Allah creates colors, movements, and qualities in bodies without being described by those qualities.

f: How is the verse about Jesus عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ creating a bird shape answered?
b: The word “create” there means forming or shaping (taqdīr), not creating from absolute non-existence.

f: What does it mean that human actions occur by Allah’s will, decree, judgment, and determination?
b: It means all human actions occur within Allah’s eternal knowledge, will, creation, and specification, while humans still possess choice and responsibility.

f: Why does Allah’s decree of disbelief not require being pleased with disbelief?
b: Because the obligation of being pleased applies to Allah’s decree (qaḍāʾ), not necessarily to the thing decreed (maqḍī). A person may dislike the existence of sin while accepting Allah’s wisdom in allowing it.

f: Why does Allah creating disbelief and sin not make people forced and unable to be commanded with faith and obedience?
b: Because Allah wills that the disbeliever and sinner choose disbelief and sin through their own choice. Allah’s will does not remove their voluntary choice, just as Allah’s knowledge of their choices does not force them.

f: How do the Muʿtazilah view Allah’s will regarding evil actions?
b: They deny that Allah wills disbelief and sins. They claim Allah only wills faith and obedience from people, and that willing evil would itself be evil.

f: What is the problem with the Muʿtazilah position regarding Allah’s will?
b: It implies that most human actions occur against Allah’s will, which would mean that created beings can bring about things that Allah does not will, contradicting His absolute sovereignty.

f: What story is mentioned about ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and the Magian?
b: ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd said no one had defeated him in argument like a Magian who was with him on a ship. When ʿAmr asked why he did not accept Islam, the Magian replied: “If Allah willed my Islam, I would become Muslim.” When ʿAmr said Allah wills your Islam but devils prevent you, the Magian replied: “Then I am with the stronger partner.”

f: What is the story of Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār and Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāʾīnī?
b: When Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār entered upon al-Ṣāḥib ibn ʿAbbād and saw Abū Isḥāq, he said: “Glory be to the One who is far above indecency.” Abū Isḥāq immediately replied: “Glory be to the One in whose dominion nothing occurs except what He wills.”

f: Why did the Muʿtazilah make faith of the unbeliever desired by Allah but disbelief undesired?
b: Because they believed that commands necessarily indicate will, and prohibitions indicate lack of will. Since Allah commands faith and forbids disbelief, they concluded He wills faith but does not will disbelief.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah respond to the claim that commands always indicate Allah’s will?
b: They say a thing may be commanded without being desired, due to wisdom and purposes known to Allah. For example, a master may command his servant to do something while intending to expose his disobedience.

f: What verse is mentioned regarding Allah not being questioned about His actions?
b: {لَا يُسْأَلُ عَمَّا يَفْعَلُ} — “He is not questioned about what He does.” (Qur’an 21:23)

f: What is the belief of Ahl al-Sunnah regarding human actions?
b: Humans possess voluntary actions. They are rewarded for obedience and punished for disobedience.

f: What did the Jabriyyah claim regarding human actions?
b: They claimed humans have no real actions, and that their movements are like the movements of inanimate objects, without ability, intention, or choice.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah refute the Jabriyyah?
b: They argue that people necessarily distinguish between voluntary movement (such as striking) and involuntary movement (such as trembling). The first occurs through choice, while the second does not.

f: Why would denying human voluntary actions invalidate religious responsibility?
b: Because commands, prohibitions, reward, punishment, and attributing intentional actions to people would have no meaning if humans had no choice.

f: What examples show the difference between voluntary and involuntary actions?
b: Saying “he prayed,” “he fasted,” or “he wrote” attributes actions involving intention and choice. Saying “the boy grew tall” or “his color became black” does not imply choice.

f: What Qur’anic verses support human choice?
b: Examples include: {جَزَاءً بِمَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ} (“as a reward for what they used to do”) and {فَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِنْ وَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ} (“Whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve”).

f: How is the objection that Allah’s complete knowledge and will imply determinism answered?
b: Allah knows and wills that the servant performs an action through his own choice. His knowledge does not compel the action; rather, He knows the action exactly as it occurs.

f: If Allah knows and wills an action, does that make the action necessary and remove choice?
b: No. Necessity according to Allah’s knowledge does not contradict human choice. An action can be certain to occur while still occurring through voluntary choice.

f: How is this compared to Allah’s own actions?
b: Allah’s knowledge and will are also related to His own actions, yet this does not mean Allah is forced. Therefore, certainty from knowledge does not eliminate choice.

f: What objection is raised regarding human beings being creators of their own actions?
b: It is argued that if being an agent means creating one’s actions through intention and power, then Allah alone creates actions. A single thing cannot be under two independent powers of creation.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah answer the objection that only Allah creates actions?
b: They affirm that Allah is the Creator of all actions, while humans are the ones who acquire (kasb) their actions through their own power and choice.

f: What is kasb (acquisition) according to this discussion?
b: It is when a servant directs his ability and intention toward an action, while Allah creates the action itself.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah reconcile Allah’s creation of actions with human responsibility?
b: The servant’s choice and intention are real and have an effect in distinguishing voluntary actions, but the actual creation and existence of the action belongs to Allah.

f: What example is given of where human ability has a role?
b: Voluntary movement such as striking with the hand occurs through human ability and intention, whereas involuntary trembling does not involve choice.

f: What is the final summary of the relationship between Allah’s creation and human action?
b: Allah is the Creator of every action, and the servant is the one who chooses and acquires the action. The same act is attributed to Allah in terms of creation and to the servant in terms of choice and acquisition.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah explain the relationship between Allah’s creation of actions and the servant’s acquisition (kasb)?
b: The action is attributed to Allah from the perspective of creation and bringing into existence, while it is attributed to the servant from the perspective of acquisition and choice. The same action is connected to both, but through two different aspects.

f: Why is the action considered Allah’s act of creation and the servant’s act of acquisition?
b: Because Allah independently creates the existence of the action, while the servant directs his ability and choice toward that action. Allah is the Creator, and the servant is the one who acquires the act.

f: What explanations did scholars give for the difference between creation (khalq) and acquisition (kasb)?
b: They said: acquisition occurs through a tool or means, while creation does not require a tool; acquisition occurs within the sphere of the servant’s power, while creation occurs beyond his power; and acquisition cannot occur independently of Allah’s creation, whereas Allah’s creation is independent.

f: Does attributing actions to both Allah and the servant mean that Ahl al-Sunnah believe in shirk?
b: No. Shirk means two beings sharing in the same matter independently, like partners sharing ownership. Here, Allah and the servant are related to the action through different aspects: Allah through creation, and the servant through acquisition.

f: What example is given to explain two different aspects of attribution?
b: An object may belong to Allah as Creator and to a servant as owner. Likewise, a servant’s action is attributed to Allah by creation and to the servant by acquisition.

f: Why is acquiring an evil action considered blameworthy, while creating it is not?
b: Because Allah is perfectly wise and creates nothing except with wisdom and beneficial consequences, even if humans do not know them. The servant, however, may choose evil despite being commanded not to, making his acquisition blameworthy.

f: How is a servant’s good action defined?
b: It is an action that deserves praise in this world and reward in the Hereafter.

f: How is a servant’s evil action defined?
b: It is an action that deserves blame in this world and punishment in the Hereafter.

f: Are all human actions by Allah’s will and pleasure?
b: All actions occur by Allah’s will, decree, and permission, but not all occur by His pleasure. Allah wills the existence of some things without approving of them.

f: What verse is mentioned to show Allah does not approve of disbelief?
b: {وَلَا يَرْضَى لِعِبَادِهِ الْكُفْرَ} — “He does not approve disbelief for His servants.” (Qur’an 39:7)

f: What is the difference between Allah’s will and His pleasure?
b: Allah’s will, decree, and determination encompass everything, including sins. His pleasure, love, and command only relate to what is good and obedient.

f: What is the view of the Muʿtazilah regarding human ability (istiṭāʿah)?
b: They held that ability exists before the action and that the servant possesses the power by which he independently performs his actions.

f: What is the view of Ahl al-Sunnah regarding istiṭāʿah?
b: The ability by which the action occurs is created by Allah and accompanies the action itself.

f: What is the first definition of istiṭāʿah mentioned here?
b: It is the actual power through which the action occurs. According to this view, it is a created attribute that accompanies the action.

f: What does the author mention regarding the creation of ability according to intention?
b: If the servant intends good, Allah creates the ability for good. If he intends evil, Allah creates the ability for evil. Therefore, the servant is responsible because the intention originates from him.

f: Why do they argue that ability must accompany the action?
b: Because ability is an accident (ʿaraḍ), and accidents cannot remain after their creation. If ability existed before the action and disappeared, the action would occur without ability.

f: How do they respond to the objection that similar abilities could be recreated continuously?
b: They say this only proves that the ability through which the action happens must be the ability present at the time of the action. If one claims there must be previous abilities before it, proof is required.

f: What problem arises if one claims an earlier ability remains until the action?
b: If the earlier ability can perform the action, then the person has abandoned the claim that ability must precede the action. If it cannot, there is no reason why it should become effective later without a change occurring in the ability itself.

f: Why do some scholars say ability can be before the action?
b: Because they argue that responsibility exists before the action. A disbeliever is commanded to believe and someone who misses prayer is commanded after the prayer time begins; therefore, ability must exist before the action.

f: How do they answer the argument that obligation requires ability before the action?
b: They explain that “ability” has different meanings. The ability required for responsibility is the availability of means, tools, and bodily capability, not necessarily the actual creative power that produces the action.

f: What does “ability” mean when mentioned in relation to Hajj?
b: It refers to having the means, resources, physical health, and necessary conditions to perform it, as in: {وَلِلَّهِ عَلَى النَّاسِ حِجُّ الْبَيْتِ مَنِ اسْتَطَاعَ إِلَيْهِ سَبِيلًا}.

f: Why can the safety of means and tools be considered part of ability even though they are not the person himself?
b: Because a person can be described as possessing sound means and tools, even though the expression is not formed as a direct attribute like “powerful.”

f: Upon which type of ability does the validity of religious responsibility depend?
b: It depends on the ability meaning soundness of means, tools, and faculties, not necessarily the created power that accompanies the action itself.

f: What is the difference between inability and lack of the first type of ability?
b: If inability means lacking the actual power that accompanies action, then it does not necessarily invalidate responsibility. If it means lacking the means and faculties needed to act, then responsibility is not valid.

f: What is the ruling regarding Allah تَعَالَى creating all the actions of His servants?
b: Allah تَعَالَى is the Creator of all the actions of His servants, including disbelief, faith, obedience, and disobedience. This is contrary to the Muʿtazilah, who claimed that the servant creates his own actions.

f: Why did some early Muʿtazilah avoid calling the servant a “creator” of his actions?
b: Because they avoided using the word “creator” and instead used terms such as “originator” and “inventor.” Later, al-Jubbāʾī and his followers argued that the meaning was the same and openly used the term “creator.”

f: What is the first proof of Ahl al-Sunnah that the servant does not create his own actions?
b: If the servant were the creator of his actions, he would necessarily know the details of those actions, because creating something through power and choice requires knowledge of it. However, a person walking does not know all the intermediate movements and still performs them.

f: What is the second proof that Allah تَعَالَى creates the actions of His servants?
b: The textual proofs, such as Allah’s saying: {وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ} — “Allah created you and what you do.” This means that Allah created both the servants and their actions.

f: How is the verse {وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ} understood?
b: If “مَا” is taken as a verbal noun, it means Allah created you and your actions. If it is taken as a relative pronoun, it means Allah created you and what you perform. Both meanings support that actions are created by Allah.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah answer the claim that believing Allah creates actions makes people polytheists?
b: They explain that shirk means affirming a partner in divinity, either in necessary existence or deserving worship. The Muʿtazilah do not claim this; however, their view wrongly gives creatures independent creative power.

f: Why did some scholars from Mā Warāʾ al-Nahr strongly criticize the Muʿtazilah on this issue?
b: They argued that the Muʿtazilah effectively affirmed countless creators because they attributed creative power to servants, whereas the Magians only affirmed one partner with Allah.

f: What proofs did the Muʿtazilah use to support their position?
b: They argued that people necessarily distinguish between voluntary movement (like walking) and involuntary movement (like trembling), and that if Allah created all actions, moral responsibility, praise, blame, reward, and punishment would become meaningless.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah respond to the Muʿtazilah argument about voluntary and involuntary actions?
b: They say this argument only applies against the Jabriyyah, who deny human choice completely. Ahl al-Sunnah affirm that humans have choice and acquisition (kasb), while Allah is the Creator of the actions.

f: Why is it incorrect to say that if Allah creates actions, then He is the one who walks, sits, eats, drinks, commits adultery, or steals?
b: Because an attribute belongs to the one in whom it exists, not the one who creates it. Allah creates colors and qualities in bodies but is not described by those qualities.

f: How is the verse {فَتَبَارَكَ اللَّهُ أَحْسَنُ الْخَالِقِينَ} regarding Jesus عليه السلام answered?
b: The word “creation” there means estimation or shaping, not actual bringing into existence from nothing.

f: What does it mean that all human actions occur by Allah’s will, decree, and judgment?
b: It means every action occurs by Allah’s will, choice, and determination. Allah’s will encompasses all things, while His pleasure is only with obedience and good actions.

f: If disbelief occurs by Allah’s decree, does that mean one must be pleased with disbelief?
b: No. One must be pleased with Allah’s decree, not necessarily with the thing decreed. Disbelief is something decreed, but the decree itself is what is attributed to Allah and must be accepted.

f: Why are disbelievers not considered forced into disbelief?
b: Because Allah willed their disbelief through their own choice. Just as Allah knows that they will choose disbelief, His knowledge does not force them into it.

f: What was the Muʿtazilah view regarding Allah’s will and evil actions?
b: They denied that Allah wills evil actions, claiming that Allah only wills faith and obedience from people.

f: How do Ahl al-Sunnah respond to the Muʿtazilah claim that willing evil is itself evil?
b: They say creating something evil is not itself evil, because Allah creates things with wisdom and purposes that may be unknown to humans. However, acquiring evil through choice deserves blame.

f: What did the story of ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and the Magian illustrate?
b: It illustrated the difficulty in the Muʿtazilah position that Allah wants everyone to believe but cannot overcome the will of others, leading the Magian to argue that he would side with the stronger partner.

f: What did al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār and Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāʾīnī say when they met?
b: Al-Qāḍī said: “Glory be to the One who is free from indecency.” Abū Isḥāq replied: “Glory be to the One in whose dominion nothing occurs except what He wills.”

f: What is the Sunni position regarding human actions?
b: Humans possess real voluntary actions. They are rewarded for obedience and punished for disobedience. This rejects both the Muʿtazilah (humans create their actions independently) and the Jabriyyah (humans have no actions at all).

f: What proofs show that humans truly have actions?
b: People naturally distinguish between voluntary and involuntary movements. Also, revelation attributes actions to humans, such as Allah’s saying: {جَزَاءً بِمَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ} and {فَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِنْ وَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ}.

f: Does Allah’s complete knowledge and will of actions eliminate human choice?
b: No. Allah knows and wills that humans perform actions by their own choice. Divine knowledge does not force the action.

f: How can an action be both created by Allah and chosen by the servant?
b: The servant directs his power and intention toward an action, and Allah creates the action after that. The action is attributed to Allah by creation and to the servant by acquisition (kasb).

f: How is the difference between creation and acquisition explained?
b: Creation occurs without a tool and belongs to Allah. Acquisition occurs through the servant’s ability and choice. The same action is connected to Allah from the perspective of creation and to the servant from the perspective of acquisition.

f: Does attributing an action to both Allah and the servant mean there are two creators?
b: No. Partnership requires two entities sharing the same function independently. Here, the attribution is from two different perspectives: Allah creates, while the servant acquires and exercises choice.

f: Why is acquiring an evil action blameworthy but creating it is not?
b: Allah is perfectly wise and creates nothing except with wisdom, even if humans do not understand it. The servant, however, may choose evil despite being prohibited from it, making his acquisition blameworthy.

f: What is the definition of a good action (ḥasan) according to this discussion?
b: A good action is one that deserves praise in this world and reward in the next.

f: What is the definition of an evil action (qabīḥ)?
b: An evil action is one that deserves blame in this world and punishment in the next.

f: Does Allah’s will apply to both good and evil actions?
b: Yes. Allah’s will, decree, and creation encompass all actions, but His pleasure and command only apply to good actions.

f: What is istitaʿah (ability/capacity) according to the author?
b: It is the ability through which an action occurs. Some scholars say it is a created attribute accompanying the action, while others say it is a condition for performing the action.

f: Is ability according to the majority before or with the action?
b: The majority of theologians say the effective ability accompanies the action, because abilities are created attributes that do not remain permanently.

f: How do scholars who say ability exists before the action respond?
b: They argue that a person must have ability before being commanded, otherwise commanding someone unable would be impossible.

f: What does the author say about the ability of a disbeliever to believe?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, the ability used for disbelief is the same ability that could have been used for faith. The difference lies only in its direction and use.

f: What does “Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity” mean?
b: Allah does not command a servant to do what is impossible for him, whether impossible in itself or impossible for him due to lacking means.

f: What is the difference between inability in itself and inability due to circumstances?
b: Some things are impossible by their nature, such as combining opposites. Others are possible in themselves but impossible for a person due to lack of ability, such as creating a body.

f: What do the Muʿtazilah and Ashʿariyyah differ on regarding commanding what is impossible?
b: The Muʿtazilah reject its possibility based on their belief in rational moral obligations. The Ashʿariyyah allow it because nothing is intrinsically binding upon Allah.

f: What is the ruling regarding pain caused by being struck or bones breaking after an injury?
b: Such things are created by Allah, and the servant has no independent role in creating them.

f: How did the Muʿtazilah explain secondary effects like pain from hitting?
b: They used the concept of tawallud (generation), saying one action generates another, such as striking causing pain and breaking causing fracture.

f: What is the Sunni response to the theory of tawallud?
b: Ahl al-Sunnah say all such effects are directly created by Allah. The servant’s role is only in acquiring the initial action.

f: What is the meaning of the statement “The one who is killed dies by his appointed time” (وَالْمَقْتُولُ مَيِّتٌ بِأَجَلِهِ)?
b: It means that the person who is killed dies at the time that Allah تَعَالَى already decreed for his death. His death was not brought forward from another appointed time.

f: What was the view of some Muʿtazilah regarding the death of the murdered person?
b: Some Muʿtazilah claimed that Allah تَعَالَى had cut short the murdered person’s lifespan, meaning that if he had not been killed, he would have lived longer.

f: What is the Sunni proof that the murdered person dies at his appointed time?
b: Allah تَعَالَى has decreed the lifespans of His servants according to His eternal knowledge, without uncertainty. Allah says that when their appointed time comes, they cannot delay it nor bring it forward even for a moment.

f: What proofs did the Muʿtazilah use to argue that the murdered person does not die at his appointed time?
b: They used narrations stating that some acts of obedience increase lifespan. They also argued that if the murdered person died by his appointed time, the killer would not deserve blame, punishment, blood money, or retaliation.

f: How is the argument about acts of obedience increasing lifespan answered?
b: Allah knew that if a person did not perform those acts, he would live for forty years, but if he performed them, he would live for seventy years. The increase is attributed to the obedience because Allah knew it would be the cause of the longer lifespan.

f: How is the argument that the killer would not deserve punishment answered?
b: The obligation of punishment, compensation, and retaliation is based on religious legislation. The killer is blameworthy because he intentionally committed a prohibited act and caused death through his own acquisition (kasb), even though Allah created the death.

f: Is death itself created by Allah or caused by the servant?
b: Death is created by Allah تَعَالَى and belongs to the deceased. The servant has no role in creating death.

f: What evidence is given that death is created?
b: Allah تعالى says: {خَلَقَ الْمَوْتَ وَالْحَيَاةَ} — “He created death and life.”

f: What difference exists among scholars regarding the nature of death?
b: The majority of theologians held that death is an absence (ʿadamī), while some held that it is an existent thing created by Allah.

f: What is the meaning of Allah creating death according to those who consider death non-existent?
b: It means Allah decreed and determined death, not that He created an independent existent entity called death.

f: Is there one appointed lifespan (ajal) or multiple lifespans?
b: There is one appointed lifespan.

f: What was al-Kaʿbī’s view regarding the lifespan of the murdered person?
b: He claimed that the murdered person has two lifespans: one if killed and another if he dies naturally. If he was not killed, he would have lived until the second lifespan.

f: What was the philosophers’ view regarding natural lifespan?
b: They claimed that animals have a natural lifespan determined by the breakdown of bodily moisture and extinguishing of innate heat, along with accidental lifespans caused by illnesses and external events.

f: What is the definition of rizq (provision) according to Ahl al-Sunnah?
b: Rizq is whatever Allah تَعَالَى brings to a creature and allows it to consume. Therefore, both lawful and unlawful food are included in rizq.

f: Why is unlawful wealth considered rizq according to Ahl al-Sunnah?
b: Because rizq is something attributed to Allah تَعَالَى as what He provides to His creatures. Unlawful consumption still occurs through what Allah has created and provided.

f: Why did the Muʿtazilah reject calling unlawful things rizq?
b: They defined rizq as either something owned by the one who consumes it or something whose benefit is unrestrictedly allowed. Since unlawful things do not meet these definitions, they denied they are rizq.

f: What problem results from the Muʿtazilah definition of rizq?
b: It would mean animals do not receive rizq, and a person who only eats unlawful things was never provided for by Allah تَعَالَى.

f: Why is a person blamed for consuming unlawful rizq even though Allah created it?
b: Because Allah created the means and the person chose to use those means improperly. The blame is due to his voluntary acquisition and choice.

f: Does every person consume all of his own allotted rizq?
b: Yes. Every person receives and consumes his own provision, whether it is lawful or unlawful.

f: Why is it impossible that a person does not consume his own rizq or that another person consumes it instead?
b: Because what Allah decreed as nourishment for a person must reach that person. However, if rizq is understood as ownership, then transfer between people is possible.

f: What does “Allah misguides whom He wills and guides whom He wills” mean?
b: It means Allah تَعَالَى creates guidance and misguidance in His servants according to His will.

f: What does guidance mean according to Ahl al-Sunnah?
b: Guidance means Allah creating the state of being guided (ihtidāʾ) in a person.

f: What does misguidance mean according to Ahl al-Sunnah?
b: Misguidance means Allah creating the state of being misguided in a person.

f: What does the qualification “whom He wills” indicate regarding guidance and misguidance?
b: It indicates that the intended meaning is not merely showing the path of truth, because that occurs for everyone. Rather, it refers to Allah creating acceptance of guidance or falling into misguidance.

f: How can guidance be attributed to the Prophet ﷺ or the Qur’an if Allah alone creates guidance?
b: It is attributed metaphorically because they are causes and means that lead people toward guidance.

f: How can misguidance be attributed to Shaytan or idols if Allah creates it?
b: It is attributed metaphorically because they are causes that lead people toward misguidance, while Allah is the ultimate Creator of all things.

f: What was the Muʿtazilah understanding of guidance?
b: They understood guidance as merely showing the correct path and explaining the truth.

f: Why is the Muʿtazilah definition of guidance rejected?
b: Because Allah says: {إِنَّكَ لَا تَهْدِي مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ} — “Indeed, you do not guide whom you love,” despite the Prophet ﷺ clearly explaining the truth and calling people toward it.

f: What does the Prophet’s ﷺ supplication “O Allah, guide my people” indicate?
b: It indicates that guidance is something beyond merely explaining the path, because the Prophet ﷺ had already explained and called them, yet he asked Allah for their guidance.

f: What is the difference between Sunni and Muʿtazilah views on guidance?
b: Ahl al-Sunnah define guidance as Allah creating guidance in the heart, while the Muʿtazilah define it as only showing the correct way.

f: What is the ruling regarding the punishment of the grave for disbelievers and sinful believers according to the author?
b: The punishment of the grave applies to disbelievers and to some sinful believers. The author specifies “some” sinful believers because Allah Most High may will to forgive some of them and not punish them.

f: What is the ruling regarding the blessing and comfort of the grave for obedient believers?
b: The enjoyment and blessing of the grave for obedient believers is affirmed, according to what Allah Most High knows and wills.

f: Why do many books mention only the punishment of the grave and not its blessings?
b: Because the narrations concerning punishment of the grave are more numerous, and because most inhabitants of graves are either disbelievers or sinners, so punishment is more commonly mentioned.

f: Who are Munkar and Nakīr?
b: They are two angels who enter the grave and question the deceased about his Lord, his religion, and his Prophet.

f: Who did some scholars say are also questioned in the grave besides adults?
b: Some scholars, such as Sayyid Abū Shujāʿ, held that children are questioned, and some also held that prophets are questioned.

f: What is the proof for the punishment and blessing of the grave?
b: They are established through transmitted proofs (samʿiyyāt), because they are possible matters that were reported by the truthful Messenger ﷺ.

f: What Qur’anic verse does the author use as evidence for punishment of the grave?
b: The verse: {النَّارُ يُعْرَضُونَ عَلَيْهَا غُدُوًّا وَعَشِيًّا وَيَوْمَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ أَدْخِلُوا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ أَشَدَّ الْعَذَابِ} (Ghafir 40:46).

f: How does the author understand the verse about Pharaoh’s people being exposed to the Fire morning and evening before the Day of Resurrection?
b: He understands it as proof of punishment before the Day of Judgment, i.e., punishment in the intermediate state of the grave.

f: What other Qur’anic verse does the author cite regarding punishment before the Resurrection?
b: {أُغْرِقُوا فَأُدْخِلُوا نَارًا} (Nūḥ 71:25), indicating that they were drowned and then entered the Fire.

f: What hadith does the author mention regarding protection from the causes of grave punishment?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: «اسْتَنْزِهُوا مِنَ الْبَوْلِ، فَإِنَّ عَامَّةَ عَذَابِ الْقَبْرِ مِنْهُ» — “Guard yourselves from urine, for most of the punishment of the grave is because of it.”

f: How does the author interpret the verse {يُثَبِّتُ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِالْقَوْلِ الثَّابِتِ} (Ibrāhīm 14:27)?
b: He mentions the interpretation that it refers to the questioning of the grave, when the believer is asked: “Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet?” and answers correctly.

f: What questions are asked by Munkar and Nakīr in the grave?
b: They ask: “Who is your Lord?”, “What is your religion?”, and “Who is your Prophet?”

f: What does the hadith of the two angels describe?
b: It describes that after burial, two angels with dark blue features come to the deceased and question him. One is called Munkar and the other Nakīr.

f: How does the author describe the grave according to the hadith?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of Hellfire.”

f: What does the author say about the number of narrations concerning the matters of the Hereafter?
b: He says that narrations concerning this subject and many matters of the Hereafter are mass-transmitted in meaning (mutawātir maʿnan), even if individual reports do not reach the level of textual mass transmission.

f: Who denied the punishment of the grave?
b: Some of the Muʿtazilah and Rāfiḍah denied it.

f: What was their argument against the punishment of the grave?
b: They argued that the dead person is like an inanimate object, having no life or perception, so punishing him would be impossible.

f: How does the author respond to the objection that the dead cannot feel punishment?
b: He says Allah Most High is capable of creating in all or some parts of the body a type of life sufficient for perceiving pain or pleasure. This does not require the complete return of the soul to the body.

f: Does experiencing punishment in the grave require visible bodily movement or outward signs?
b: No. A person may be punished without visible signs appearing, just as a drowned person, someone eaten by animals, or someone crucified in the air may experience punishment even though people do not perceive it.

f: Why should one not consider punishment of the grave impossible?
b: Because when one reflects on the wonders of Allah’s dominion and the vastness of His power, such matters should not be considered impossible.

f: What is the ruling regarding the weighing of deeds (al-mīzān)?
b: The author begins the next section by affirming that the weighing of deeds is true and established.

f: Why did the author discuss the matters of the grave separately before discussing the events of the Hereafter?
b: Because the matters of the grave are intermediate between the affairs of this world and the Hereafter. After mentioning them, he proceeds to explain the reality of resurrection and the details of the Hereafter.

f: What is the proof for the realities of the grave and the Hereafter?
b: They are possible matters that were reported by the truthful Prophet ﷺ and mentioned in the Qur’an and Sunnah, therefore they are affirmed.

f: What is meant by resurrection (al-baʿth)?
b: It is that Allah Most High raises the dead from their graves by gathering their original bodily parts and returning their souls to them.

f: What is the ruling regarding resurrection?
b: Resurrection is true and must be believed in.

f: What Qur’anic proofs does the author mention for resurrection?
b: The verses: {ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ تُبْعَثُونَ} (al-Mu’minūn 23:16) and {قُلْ يُحْيِيهَا الَّذِي أَنْشَأَهَا أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ} (Yā Sīn 36:79).

f: Who denied bodily resurrection according to the author?
b: The philosophers denied it, based on their claim that the exact recreation of something after its destruction is impossible.

f: How does the author respond to the philosophers’ objection regarding resurrection?
b: He says the intended meaning is that Allah gathers the original parts of the human being and returns the soul to them. Whether this is called “recreating the exact same thing” or not is only a matter of terminology.

f: How does the author answer the objection of a person being eaten by another person?
b: He says resurrection concerns the original essential parts of the person that remain throughout his life. The consumed parts are additional parts and not the original essential body.

f: Does resurrection imply reincarnation (tanāsukh)?
b: No. Reincarnation would only follow if the second body were not created from the original parts of the first body. Calling resurrection “reincarnation” would merely be a dispute over terminology.

f: What is the ruling regarding the weighing of deeds (al-mīzān)?
b: The weighing of deeds is true and must be believed in.

f: What evidence does the author mention for the weighing of deeds?
b: The verse: {وَالْوَزْنُ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْحَقُّ} (al-Aʿrāf 7:8).

f: What is meant by the “balance” (mīzān)?
b: It refers to something by which the amounts and measures of deeds are known. Its exact reality is beyond human understanding.

f: Why did the Muʿtazilah reject the weighing of deeds?
b: They argued that deeds are accidents (aʿrāḍ) and cannot be weighed, and if Allah recreates them for weighing, then weighing them would be pointless.

f: How does the author respond to the Muʿtazilah’s objection about weighing deeds?
b: He says reports mention that the records of deeds may be what are weighed. Also, even if deeds themselves are weighed, Allah’s actions contain wisdoms that humans may not know. Lack of knowing the wisdom does not make something meaningless.

f: What is the ruling regarding the record of deeds (al-kitāb)?
b: The record containing the servants’ good deeds and sins is true.

f: What happens to the record of deeds of believers and disbelievers?
b: Believers receive their records in their right hands, while disbelievers receive them in their left hands or from behind their backs.

f: What Qur’anic evidence does the author give for the record of deeds?
b: {وَنُخْرِجُ لَهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ كِتَابًا يَلْقَاهُ مَنْشُورًا} (al-Isrāʾ 17:13) and {فَأَمَّا مَنْ أُوتِيَ كِتَابَهُ بِيَمِينِهِ فَسَوْفَ يُحَاسَبُ حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا} (al-Inshiqāq 84:7–8).

f: Why did some Muʿtazilah reject the record of deeds?
b: They claimed it was meaningless and without purpose. The author responds that Allah’s actions may contain wisdoms unknown to people.

f: What is the ruling regarding questioning on the Day of Judgment?
b: The questioning is true and established.

f: What Qur’anic evidence does the author mention for questioning?
b: {فَلَنَسْأَلَنَّ أَجْمَعِينَ} (al-Ḥijr 15:92).

f: How is the questioning of believers described in the hadith mentioned?
b: Allah brings the believer close, covers him with His protection, and privately reminds him of his sins. The believer acknowledges them, then Allah says that He concealed them in this world and forgives him that day.

f: How are the disbelievers and hypocrites treated during questioning?
b: They are called out publicly before all creation.

f: What is the ruling regarding the Prophet’s ﷺ Pool (al-Ḥawḍ)?
b: The Pool is true and must be believed in.

f: What evidence does the author mention for the Pool?
b: The verse {إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ الْكَوْثَرَ} (al-Kawthar 108:1) and the many hadiths describing the Prophet’s ﷺ Pool.

f: How is the Prophet’s ﷺ Pool described?
b: Its length is a month’s journey, its corners are equal, its water is whiter than milk, its fragrance is better than musk, and its cups are more numerous than the stars of the sky. Whoever drinks from it will never become thirsty again.

f: What is the ruling regarding the Ṣirāṭ (bridge over Hell)?
b: The Ṣirāṭ is true and must be believed in.

f: What is the Ṣirāṭ according to the author?
b: It is a bridge stretched over Hell, thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword. The people of Paradise cross it, while the feet of the people of Hell slip from it.

f: Who rejected the Ṣirāṭ according to the author?
b: Most of the Muʿtazilah rejected it.

f: Why did the Muʿtazilah reject the Ṣirāṭ?
b: They argued that crossing such a bridge would be impossible. (The author continues to answer this objection in the following passage.)

f: How does the author respond to the Muʿtazilah objection that the Ṣirāṭ is impossible to cross?
b: He responds that Allah Most High is capable of enabling people to cross it and making it easy for the believers, just as the hadiths describe different speeds of crossing.

f: What are the different speeds at which believers cross the Ṣirāṭ according to the hadiths?
b: Some believers cross like a flashing lightning bolt, some like a swift wind, some like a fast horse, and others according to their deeds.

f: What is the ruling regarding Paradise and Hell?
b: Paradise and Hell are real and must be believed in.

f: What is the evidence for the existence of Paradise and Hell?
b: The Qur’anic verses and hadiths regarding them are so well-known and numerous that they cannot be denied.

f: What objection did those who denied Paradise’s existence in its present form raise?
b: They argued that Paradise is described as having a width like the heavens and the earth, which they considered impossible in the physical world.

f: How does the author answer the objection regarding the vastness of Paradise?
b: He says this objection is based on a false philosophical premise. Allah’s power is not restricted by the limitations of the physical world.

f: Are Paradise and Hell created already or will they only be created on the Day of Judgment?
b: According to the author, Paradise and Hell are already created and currently exist.

f: Who claimed that Paradise and Hell will only be created at the time of recompense?
b: Most of the Muʿtazilah held that they would only be created on the Day of Judgment.

f: What evidence does the author provide that Paradise already exists?
b: He cites the story of Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ عَلَيْهِمَا السَّلَامُ, who were placed in Paradise, and the verses describing Paradise as already prepared for the believers.

f: What Qur’anic verses does the author mention proving that Paradise and Hell are prepared already?
b: {أُعِدَّتْ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ} (Āl ʿImrān 3:133) — “prepared for the God-fearing,” and {أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكَافِرِينَ} (al-Baqarah 2:24) — “prepared for the disbelievers.”

f: How does the author respond to the argument that Paradise cannot already exist because Allah says: {تِلْكَ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ} (“That is the Hereafter’s abode”)?
b: He says this can refer to its state and permanence, not necessarily that it does not currently exist. Also, the story of Ādam remains evidence that Paradise existed before.

f: What objection do the Muʿtazilah raise regarding Paradise being created now?
b: They argue that if Paradise already exists, it would be subject to destruction, because Allah says: {كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ} (“Everything will perish except His Face”).

f: How does the author respond to the argument that Paradise must perish?
b: He says the meaning of the permanence of Paradise’s fruits is not that the same physical fruit remains forever, but that whenever something is consumed, Allah replaces it with another.

f: Does destruction (halāk) necessarily mean complete annihilation?
b: No. The author says destruction can mean losing the ability to benefit from something, not necessarily total non-existence.

f: How else does the author interpret {كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ}?
b: He says it may mean that every possible thing is “perishing” in itself when compared to Allah’s necessary existence, because only Allah’s existence is necessary and everlasting.

f: What is meant by the statement: "The actions of the servants are voluntary"?
b: It means that humans possess actions which they perform through choice and intention. Therefore, they can be commanded and held accountable for their obedience and disobedience.

f: Why does the author reject the view of the Jabriyyah (determinists) that servants have no real actions?
b: Because if humans had no actions of their own and their movements were like the movements of inanimate objects, then religious obligations, reward, punishment, and attributing actions such as "he prayed", "he fasted", and "he wrote" to them would not be meaningful.

f: How do we know that humans have voluntary actions?
b: We necessarily distinguish between voluntary movements, such as striking with the hand, and involuntary movements, such as trembling. The first occurs by choice while the second does not.

f: What is the argument that complete belief in Allah's knowledge and will leads to determinism?
b: It is argued that since Allah knows and wills all actions, those actions must either occur necessarily if they are willed, or be impossible if they are not willed. Therefore, there would be no choice.

f: How does the author answer the argument that Allah's knowledge and will necessitate compulsion?
b: He answers that Allah knows and wills that the servant performs the action through his own choice. The servant's choosing is itself part of Allah's knowledge and will.

f: Does something being known by Allah mean it is forced?
b: No. Allah knows that a person will choose an action freely; His knowledge does not compel the person.

f: How do the Ash‘aris explain human action while maintaining that Allah is the Creator of all things?
b: They say Allah creates the action, while the servant acquires (kasb) the action through his power and choice.

f: What is meant by "kasb" (acquisition)?
b: Kasb is when the servant directs his ability and intention toward an action, while Allah creates the actual occurrence of that action.

f: How can one action belong to both Allah and the servant?
b: It belongs to Allah in terms of creation (khalq), and to the servant in terms of acquisition and choice (kasb). These are two different aspects, not a partnership in creation.

f: Why is there no contradiction in saying Allah creates evil actions but the servant is punished for them?
b: Allah's creation of the action is based on His wisdom, while the servant's choice and acquisition of the evil action makes him deserving of blame and punishment.

f: Why is creating something evil not itself evil when done by Allah?
b: Because Allah is perfectly wise and does not create anything except with wisdom and a beneficial consequence, even if humans do not perceive it.

f: Why is acquiring an evil action blameworthy for humans?
b: Because humans choose evil despite being commanded to avoid it. Their choice of evil is therefore foolish and deserving of blame.

f: What is the definition of a good action according to the author?
b: A good action is one that deserves praise in this world and reward in the Hereafter.

f: What is the definition of an evil action according to the author?
b: An evil action is one that deserves blame in this world and punishment in the Hereafter.

f: Does Allah's will include evil actions?
b: Yes. Allah's will and decree encompass everything, including evil actions, but His pleasure and command only relate to what is good.

f: What is the difference between Allah's will and Allah's pleasure?
b: Allah may will something to occur according to His wisdom, while not being pleased with it. For example, sins occur by His will but He does not love or approve of them.

f: What is meant by "ability (istita‘ah) is with the action"?
b: According to the Ash‘ari position, the complete ability that produces an action exists together with the action itself.

f: What is the difference between the two meanings of ability?
b: One meaning is the general ability consisting of sound limbs, means, and circumstances; this exists before the action. The other is the actual power by which the action occurs; this accompanies the action.

f: Why do the Ash‘aris say the actual ability accompanies the action?
b: Because abilities are created attributes that do not remain from one moment to another. Therefore, the ability present when the action occurs must exist at that same time.

f: What is the objection that arises regarding ability and responsibility?
b: If ability only exists with the action, then how can someone be commanded before performing it, such as a disbeliever being commanded to believe?

f: How does the author answer the objection about responsibility before action?
b: He says the ability required for obligation is not necessarily the actual power producing the action, but rather the soundness of means, limbs, and circumstances.

f: What does "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity" mean?
b: It means Allah does not obligate a person with something impossible for them to perform.

f: Did the Ash‘aris believe Allah could command what is impossible?
b: The Ash‘aris differed: many held that Allah's wisdom prevents such obligation, while theoretically Allah is not restricted by human concepts of obligation.

f: Why do the Mu‘tazilah reject the possibility of Allah commanding the impossible?
b: Because they believe reason determines that such an act would be morally wrong and therefore impossible for Allah.

f: What is the Ash‘ari response to the argument from the verse "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity"?
b: They say the verse indicates what Allah actually does, not necessarily a rational impossibility. Allah's actions are not judged by external obligations.

f: What is the meaning of "the murdered person dies by his appointed term"?
b: The murdered person's death occurs at the time Allah decreed for his death, not before or after it.

f: How did some Mu‘tazilah explain the death of a murdered person?
b: They claimed that Allah had appointed another lifespan for him, but the murderer shortened it by killing him.

f: How does the author respond to the claim that obedience increases lifespan?
b: Allah already knows that if a person performs certain acts of obedience, he will live longer. The increase is attributed to the obedience because Allah's knowledge includes that condition.

f: Why is the murderer punished if the murdered person died at his appointed time?
b: Because punishment is based on the murderer's sinful action and intention, even though Allah created the death that followed it.

f: What is meant by "the appointed term (ajal) is one"?
b: Every person has one fixed appointed time of death, not multiple possible terms.

f: What is the belief of the Mu‘tazilah regarding halal and haram provision?
b: They generally held that unlawful food is not considered rizq (provision) because rizq must be something lawful.

f: Why does the author say unlawful things are still rizq?
b: Because rizq is what Allah brings to a creature and allows it to consume, whether it is halal or haram.

f: What does it mean that Allah guides and misguides whom He wills?
b: It means Allah creates guidance and misguidance. Guidance is not merely showing the path, because Allah showed the path even to those who were not guided.

f: What is the Sunni definition of guidance?
b: Guidance is Allah creating the state of being guided in a person.

f: What is the Mu‘tazilah definition of guidance?
b: Guidance is merely showing the correct path and explaining the truth.

f: Why do Sunnis reject the Mu‘tazilah definition of guidance?
b: Because Allah says to the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, you do not guide whom you love," even though the Prophet ﷺ explained the truth and called people toward it.

f: Is Allah obligated to do what is best (al-aslah) for His servants?
b: No. According to Sunni theology, Allah is not obligated to do what humans consider most beneficial.

f: Why do the Mu‘tazilah believe Allah must do what is best?
b: Because they believe abandoning what is best would be foolish or unjust, and they consider rational ethics binding upon Allah.

f: How do Sunnis respond to the doctrine of obligation of the best?
b: They say Allah is already proven to be perfectly wise and generous; nothing external obligates Him.

f: Is the punishment of the grave true?
b: Yes. The author states that punishment of the grave occurs for disbelievers and some sinful believers.

f: Is enjoyment in the grave also affirmed?
b: Yes. The author affirms that righteous people receive blessing and comfort in the grave.

f: Who are Munkar and Nakir?
b: They are two angels who enter the grave and question the deceased about his Lord, religion, and Prophet.

f: What is the evidence for the questioning of the grave?
b: It is established through authentic transmitted texts from the Qur'an and Sunnah.

f: What is the Sunni response to those who reject punishment of the grave because the dead cannot perceive?
b: Allah is capable of creating a type of life in the body parts sufficient for perception of pain or pleasure, without requiring the soul to return fully to the body.

f: Is resurrection true according to Sunni belief?
b: Yes. Allah will resurrect the dead by gathering their original bodily parts and returning their souls to them.

f: Why did philosophers reject bodily resurrection?
b: They argued that resurrection requires bringing back the same destroyed body, which they considered impossible.

f: How does the author answer the objection about bodily resurrection?
b: He explains that resurrection concerns the original essential parts of the body, not every temporary part acquired during life.

f: Is the weighing of deeds true?
b: Yes. The Qur'an and Sunnah affirm that deeds will be weighed on the Day of Judgment.

f: What is the objection of the Mu‘tazilah regarding weighing deeds?
b: They argued that deeds are temporary accidents and cannot be weighed, making the act meaningless.

f: How does the author respond regarding the weighing of deeds?
b: He says the texts indicate that the records of deeds may be weighed, and Allah may have wisdoms behind the weighing that humans do not know.

f: Is the record of deeds true?
b: Yes. Every person's deeds are recorded and their book will be given to them on the Day of Judgment.

f: Is questioning on the Day of Judgment true?
b: Yes. Allah will question His creation, and believers may receive a private questioning involving forgiveness and concealment of their sins.

f: Is the Hawd (Prophetic Pool) true?
b: Yes. The Prophet ﷺ will have a pool whose water is whiter than milk and whose drinkers will never thirst afterward.

f: Is the Sirat bridge true?
b: Yes. It is a bridge over Hell that people will cross according to their deeds.

f: Are Paradise and Hell created already?
b: Yes. The author affirms that Paradise and Hell currently exist.

f: Why do the Mu‘tazilah reject that Paradise and Hell already exist?
b: They argue they should only be created at the time of reward and punishment.

f: What is the Sunni evidence that Paradise and Hell already exist?
b: The story of Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ and Hawwa being placed in Paradise and Qur'anic verses stating they have been prepared for believers and disbelievers.

f: Will Paradise and Hell ever cease to exist?
b: No. They and their inhabitants remain forever.

f: What is the Sunni position regarding the major sinner (murtakib al-kabirah)?
b: A believer who commits a major sin does not leave Islam and does not become a disbeliever.

f: What is the position of the Mu‘tazilah regarding the major sinner?
b: They say the major sinner is neither believer nor disbeliever, but occupies an intermediate position.

f: What is the position of the Khawarij regarding the major sinner?
b: They consider the major sinner a disbeliever.

f: Why do Sunnis say a major sinner remains a believer?
b: Because faith is fundamentally belief in the heart, and committing a sin does not remove belief unless it involves denial or rejection.

f: When does committing a sin become disbelief?
b: When it involves denying the religion, rejecting what is known necessarily, or showing disbelief through actions that indicate denial.

f: What evidence do Sunnis use that sinful people can still be believers?
b: Qur'anic verses addressing sinners as believers, such as the verses about retaliation and reconciliation between fighting believers.

f: How do Sunnis answer the Mu‘tazilah argument that the Qur'an contrasts believer and sinner?
b: They explain that "sinner" in those verses refers to the disbeliever, or that the wording is used for emphasis and warning.

f: How do Sunnis answer the hadith "The fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer"?
b: They explain it as a warning showing the weakness and deficiency of faith during sin, not the complete removal of faith.

f: Does Allah forgive shirk (associating partners with Him)?
b: No. Allah does not forgive shirk if a person dies upon it. This is agreed upon by the Muslims.

f: Did scholars differ regarding whether forgiving shirk is rationally possible?
b: Yes. Some said it is rationally possible but Allah informed us through revelation that He does not do so. Others said it is rationally impossible because of divine wisdom.

f: Why did some scholars say forgiveness of shirk is rationally impossible?
b: Because wisdom requires distinguishing between the obedient and the sinful. Disbelief is the greatest crime and cannot be treated like other sins that may be pardoned.

f: Why is shirk considered different from other sins regarding forgiveness?
b: Because the disbeliever considers his disbelief to be correct and does not seek forgiveness for it. Also, disbelief involves an eternal rejection, so it deserves an eternal punishment.

f: What is the Sunni position regarding forgiveness of sins less than shirk?
b: Allah may forgive any sin less than shirk, whether major or minor, with or without repentance, according to His will.

f: What verse is used as evidence that Allah forgives sins besides shirk?
b: The verse: {إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَغْفِرُ أَنْ يُشْرَكَ بِهِ وَيَغْفِرُ مَا دُونَ ذَلِكَ لِمَنْ يَشَاءُ} — "Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills."

f: How do the Mu‘tazilah interpret the verse about forgiveness of sins besides shirk?
b: They restrict it to minor sins and major sins that are accompanied by repentance.

f: What evidence do the Mu‘tazilah use to argue that major sinners must be punished?
b: They rely on verses and hadiths containing threats of punishment for sinners.

f: How do Sunnis answer the Mu‘tazilah argument from texts of punishment?
b: They say that texts of warning do not necessarily mean punishment must occur. Other texts establish Allah's forgiveness, so the texts of warning are specified by Allah's mercy.

f: Is it permissible for Allah to forgive without punishment despite warnings?
b: Yes. Sunni scholars say forgiveness is possible, and Allah's forgiveness does not contradict His promises because the warnings do not require punishment in every case.

f: Why do the Mu‘tazilah object to the possibility of forgiveness?
b: They argue that if sinners know forgiveness is possible, they may become encouraged to sin, which would contradict the purpose of sending prophets.

f: How do Sunnis answer the argument that forgiveness encourages sin?
b: They say the possibility of forgiveness does not make a person certain they will be forgiven. The strong warnings and fear of punishment remain effective deterrents.

f: Is punishment for minor sins possible?
b: Yes. Allah may punish for minor sins, whether or not the person avoids major sins.

f: What evidence is given that even minor sins may be punished?
b: The verse: {لَا يُغَادِرُ صَغِيرَةً وَلَا كَبِيرَةً إِلَّا أَحْصَاهَا} — "It leaves neither a small nor a great matter except that it has recorded it."

f: What did some Mu‘tazilah say regarding someone who avoids major sins?
b: They said such a person cannot be punished, based on the verse: {إِنْ تَجْتَنِبُوا كَبَائِرَ مَا تُنْهَوْنَ عَنْهُ نُكَفِّرْ عَنْكُمْ سَيِّئَاتِكُمْ}.

f: How do Sunnis respond to the argument that avoiding major sins guarantees no punishment?
b: They explain that the greatest major sin is disbelief, and the verse is understood in relation to sins other than disbelief.

f: Why does the author mention forgiveness of major sins again?
b: To clarify that leaving punishment for a sin is called both "forgiveness" (ʿafw) and "pardoning" (maghfirah), and to explain that forgiveness does not include sins committed through rejecting Allah's commands.

f: When does committing a major sin become disbelief?
b: When it is done through istihlāl (considering the prohibited act lawful), because this involves rejecting the divine ruling and contradicting faith.

f: What is the Sunni position regarding intercession (shafāʿah)?
b: Intercession is true and will occur for people of major sins through the prophets and righteous people.

f: Who rejects intercession for major sinners?
b: The Mu‘tazilah reject it because they deny that major sinners may be forgiven without punishment.

f: Why do Sunnis affirm intercession?
b: Because many transmitted reports establish it, and if forgiveness is possible directly from Allah, then it is even more possible through intercession.

f: What Qur'anic evidence is given for the existence of intercession?
b: The verse: {وَاسْتَغْفِرْ لِذَنْبِكَ وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ} — "Seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women."

f: What does the verse {فَمَا تَنْفَعُهُمْ شَفَاعَةُ الشَّافِعِينَ} prove?
b: It proves that intercession exists in general, because denying its benefit for disbelievers only makes sense if intercession itself exists.

f: Why does saying that intercession does not benefit disbelievers not mean it does not exist?
b: Because the verse negates its benefit for a specific group (disbelievers), not its existence altogether.

f: What is the ruling regarding Allah not forgiving shirk?
b: Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, by the consensus of the Muslims. However, they differed whether this is rationally possible or impossible.

f: Why did some scholars say Allah cannot forgive shirk rationally?
b: They argued that wisdom requires distinction between the sinner and the righteous. Disbelief is the greatest crime and cannot be treated with pardon because it removes the basis of obligation and punishment.

f: What arguments were given that a disbeliever does not deserve forgiveness?
b: A disbeliever considers his disbelief to be true and does not seek forgiveness for it, and disbelief is an eternal belief which necessitates an eternal punishment, unlike other sins.

f: What is the Sunni position regarding Allah forgiving sins other than shirk?
b: Allah forgives whatever is less than shirk, whether major or minor sins, for whom He wills, whether they repented or not.

f: What is the Mu‘tazilah position regarding forgiveness of sins other than shirk?
b: They restrict forgiveness to minor sins and major sins accompanied by repentance.

f: How do the Mu‘tazilah argue against forgiveness of major sins without repentance?
b: They cite texts threatening sinners with punishment and argue that allowing forgiveness would encourage people to sin.

f: How is the Sunni response to the Mu‘tazilah argument from texts of punishment?
b: Even if those texts are general, they indicate that punishment may occur, not that it must occur. The many texts proving forgiveness specify who is excluded from the general threats.
