f: How do scholars respond to the claim that Allah forgiving a sinner would encourage sin?
b: The possibility of forgiveness does not make a person certain that he will not be punished. The verses of warning and severe threats remain a deterrent.

f: Is punishment for minor sins possible?
b: Yes. Allah may punish for minor sins, whether or not the person avoided major sins, because they are included under the general texts of punishment.

f: What did some Mu‘tazilah say about someone who avoids major sins?
b: Some said that if a person avoids major sins, it is not permissible for Allah to punish him, based on texts promising forgiveness of sins for those who avoid major sins.

f: How is the Mu‘tazilah argument about avoiding major sins answered?
b: The absolute greatest sin is disbelief, since it is the highest form of wrongdoing. Therefore, the texts about avoiding major sins apply with respect to sins other than disbelief.

f: What is meant by forgiveness (‘afw) for major sins?
b: Forgiveness means leaving punishment for the sin, and it only applies when the sin was not committed while considering it lawful. Making a sin lawful is disbelief because it contradicts belief.

f: Who receives intercession according to Sunni belief?
b: Intercession is established for the prophets and righteous people on behalf of the people of major sins among the believers.

f: What evidence proves intercession?
b: Allah says: {وَاسْتَغْفِرْ لِذَنْبِكَ وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ} and {فَمَا تَنْفَعُهُمْ شَفَاعَةُ الشَّافِعِينَ}. The Prophet ﷺ said: “My intercession is for the people of major sins from my nation.”

f: How do the Mu‘tazilah argue against intercession?
b: They cite verses such as {وَاتَّقُوا يَوْمًا لَا تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَنْ نَفْسٍ شَيْئًا وَلَا يُقْبَلُ مِنْهَا شَفَاعَةٌ} and claim there is no intercession for sinners.

f: How is the Mu‘tazilah argument against intercession answered?
b: These verses are understood as referring to disbelievers. They are reconciled with the numerous texts establishing intercession for believers.

f: What is the ruling regarding believers who commit major sins and die without repentance?
b: They are not eternally punished in Hell.

f: What evidence proves that believers who commit major sins are not eternally in Hell?
b: Allah says: {فَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا يَرَهُ}. Since faith itself is a good deed, a believer must eventually see its reward. Eternal punishment followed by Paradise is impossible by consensus.

f: What other evidence proves believers enter Paradise?
b: Allah says: {وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ جَنَّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِنْ تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهَارُ} and {إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ كَانَتْ لَهُمْ جَنَّاتُ الْفِرْدَوْسِ نُزُلًا}.

f: Why would eternal punishment of a believer contradict justice?
b: Eternal punishment is the greatest punishment and was made the consequence of disbelief, the greatest crime. Punishing someone other than a disbeliever eternally would exceed the measure of the crime.

f: What is the Mu‘tazilah position regarding the major sinner who dies without repentance?
b: They say he remains eternally in Hell because he deserves punishment and cannot receive eternal reward.

f: How is the Mu‘tazilah argument about eternal punishment answered?
b: Punishment is not something Allah is obligated to give; reward is a favor from Allah while punishment is justice. Allah may forgive or punish for a period and then admit the person into Paradise.

f: How are verses mentioning eternal punishment for sinners understood?
b: They refer to disbelievers, such as one who kills a believer because he is a believer, rejects all Allah’s limits, or whose sins completely encompass him through disbelief.

f: What is the linguistic meaning of īmān (faith)?
b: In language, īmān means affirmation and acceptance of the truthfulness of a report or person.

f: What is the difference between mere recognition and true linguistic belief?
b: True belief is not simply knowing that something is true; it includes acceptance and submission to that truth.

f: What is the Sharī‘ah definition of īmān?
b: Īmān is believing in the heart what the Prophet ﷺ brought from Allah regarding matters known necessarily to be from Allah.

f: Is general belief sufficient for īmān?
b: Yes. General belief in all that is necessarily known to have come from Allah is sufficient and does not decrease from detailed belief.

f: Why is a person who believes in Allah but commits shirk not considered a believer Islamically?
b: Because although he may affirm the existence of the Creator, he has failed to affirm tawḥīd, which is part of what the Prophet ﷺ brought.

f: Is verbal declaration part of īmān?
b: Verbal declaration is a part of īmān, but heart affirmation is the essential pillar. Verbal declaration may be excused, such as under coercion.

f: How is it answered that belief disappears during sleep or heedlessness?
b: The belief remains in the heart; only awareness of it disappears. Even if that were not accepted, the Lawgiver treats established belief that has not been contradicted as remaining.

f: What is the definition of īmān according to some scholars such as Shams al-A’immah and Fakhr al-Islām?
b: They define īmān as both affirmation (taṣdīq) and verbal declaration (iqrār).

f: What is the definition of īmān according to the majority of the verified scholars?
b: The majority of scholars define īmān as affirmation of the heart (taṣdīq bi’l-qalb), while verbal declaration is only a condition for applying worldly rulings.

f: Why is verbal declaration considered a condition for applying worldly rulings of faith?
b: Because inner belief in the heart is hidden, so an outward sign is needed for people to judge a person’s faith.

f: What is the ruling before Allah of a person who believes in the heart but cannot verbally declare faith?
b: Such a person is a believer before Allah, even though worldly rulings of faith may not be applied to him.

f: What is the ruling of a person who verbally declares faith but does not believe in the heart?
b: Such a person is like a hypocrite: he is treated outwardly as a believer but is not a believer before Allah.

f: Which scholar’s view regarding īmān is mentioned as being chosen by Abū Manṣūr?
b: Abū Manṣūr (رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ) chose the view that īmān is affirmation of the heart.

f: What Qur’anic verse indicates that īmān is placed in the heart?
b: Allah says: {أُولَئِكَ كَتَبَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْإِيمَانَ}.

f: What Qur’anic verse indicates that faith is connected to the heart rather than merely the tongue?
b: Allah says: {وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ}.

f: What Qur’anic verse proves that a person can have faith in the heart while being forced to speak words of disbelief?
b: Allah says: {إِلَّا مَنْ أُكْرِهَ وَقَلْبُهُ مُطْمَئِنٌّ بِالْإِيمَانِ}.

f: What did the Prophet ﷺ teach about the heart and faith in his supplication?
b: He said: “O Allah, make my heart firm upon Your religion and obedience.”

f: What lesson did the Prophet ﷺ teach Usāmah ibn Zayd when he killed someone who had said “lā ilāha illā Allāh”?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “Did you split open his heart?” meaning that inner faith cannot be judged merely by outward statements.

f: Why is saying the shahādah alone not sufficient to prove true faith before Allah?
b: Because true faith requires heart affirmation, and merely speaking words does not necessarily indicate belief.

f: What Qur’anic verse proves that some people say “we believe” but are not truly believers?
b: Allah says: {وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَقُولُ آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَبِالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَمَا هُمْ بِمُؤْمِنِينَ}.

f: What Qur’anic verse distinguishes between Islam and true īmān?
b: Allah says: {قُلْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا أَسْلَمْنَا}.

f: Is a person who only declares faith verbally called a believer linguistically?
b: Yes, such a person is called a believer linguistically and receives the outward rulings of Islam.

f: What is the disagreement regarding a person who only declares faith verbally?
b: The disagreement is whether such a person is truly a believer between himself and Allah.

f: How do the rulings applied to hypocrites prove that verbal declaration alone is insufficient for true faith?
b: The Prophet ﷺ and the Companions treated hypocrites outwardly according to their statements but knew they were not believers before Allah.

f: What proves that heart affirmation is sufficient for true faith when verbal declaration is impossible?
b: The scholars agree that someone who believes in his heart and intends to declare faith but is prevented by an obstacle, such as inability to speak, is a believer.

f: What is the rejected view of the Karrāmiyyah regarding īmān?
b: They claimed that īmān is only the two statements of the shahādah.

f: What three components of īmān are mentioned as the view of many theologians, hadith scholars, and jurists?
b: They say īmān consists of belief in the heart, declaration by the tongue, and actions of the limbs.

f: What does the author state about the relationship between actions and īmān?
b: He states that actions increase and decrease in themselves, but īmān itself does not increase or decrease.

f: Why does the author argue that righteous actions are not part of the essence of īmān?
b: Because the essence of īmān is affirmation, and the Qur’an frequently mentions faith and actions separately.

f: How does the Qur’anic phrase {إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ} prove that actions are distinct from īmān?
b: The conjunction “and” indicates distinction between faith and righteous deeds.

f: How does the verse {وَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصَّالِحَاتِ ... وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ} show that actions are not part of the essence of īmān?
b: It makes faith a condition for righteous deeds, showing that faith exists separately from actions.

f: How does the verse {وَإِنْ طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا} prove that sinners can still be believers?
b: Allah called both fighting groups believers despite their grave sin of fighting one another.

f: Against which group are the arguments that actions are not part of the essence of īmān directed?
b: They are directed against the Mu‘tazilah, who considered actions a necessary part of the essence of faith.

f: How does the view of Imām al-Shāfiʿī differ from the Mu‘tazilah regarding actions and īmān?
b: Imām al-Shāfiʿī considered actions part of complete faith, but abandoning actions does not remove a person from the foundation of faith.

f: According to the view that īmān is heartly affirmation (taṣdīq), does īmān increase or decrease?
b: According to this view, īmān itself does not increase or decrease because its reality is heartly affirmation that has reached certainty and submission. Once a person has true affirmation, performing acts of obedience or committing sins does not alter the existence of that affirmation.

f: Why does the view that īmān is heartly affirmation say that a believer's faith remains unchanged despite sins and acts of obedience?
b: Because the essence of īmān is the certainty and acceptance in the heart, and this inner affirmation remains present even if a person later commits sins or performs additional acts of worship.

f: How does Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ explain the Quranic verses that mention an increase in īmān?
b: He explains that believers originally possessed general faith, then whenever a new obligation was revealed they believed in that specific obligation. Therefore, their faith increased due to the increase of matters that required belief.

f: What criticism is made against Abū Ḥanīfah's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ explanation of the increase of īmān?
b: It is objected that learning detailed religious obligations is possible even after the time of the Prophet ﷺ, so the increase of faith cannot be restricted only to the period of revelation.

f: What is the difference between general faith (īmān ijmālī) and detailed faith (īmān tafṣīlī)?
b: General faith is believing in everything that is known generally to have come from Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, while detailed faith is believing in specific matters individually as they become known.

f: Why is detailed faith considered greater than general faith?
b: Because detailed faith contains knowledge and affirmation of more specific matters, making it more complete, although general faith is still sufficient for the basic reality of being a believer.

f: How do some scholars explain the increase of īmān through the passing of time?
b: They say faith increases through remaining constant and continuously renewed at every moment, because a person's faith continues through the renewal of similar states.

f: What objection is raised against saying that faith increases because it continues over time?
b: The objection is that the renewal of a similar state after the previous one ends is not considered an increase. For example, renewing the blackness of an object does not mean its blackness has increased.

f: How do some scholars explain the increase and decrease of īmān through righteous actions and sins?
b: They explain that the essence of faith remains the same, but its fruits, light, and effect upon the heart increase through obedience and decrease through sins.

f: Why is the ability of īmān to increase and decrease obvious according to those who include actions within īmān?
b: Because actions themselves increase and decrease, and if actions are part of the reality of īmān, then īmān must also increase and decrease.

f: What argument do some scholars give that heartly affirmation itself can increase and decrease?
b: They argue that affirmation differs in strength, because the certainty of ordinary believers is not equal to the certainty of the Prophets. They cite the statement of Ibrāhīm عليه السلام: ﴿وَلـَكِنْ ل ِي َطْمَئ ِنّ ق َل ْبِيْ﴾.

f: What did some of the Qadariyyah claim was the definition of īmān?
b: They claimed that īmān is merely knowledge (maʿrifah).

f: Why is the claim that īmān is only knowledge rejected by scholars?
b: Because some people possess knowledge of the truth but still reject it. The People of the Book knew the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, and some disbelievers recognized the truth with certainty, yet they remained disbelievers because they lacked acceptance and affirmation.

f: What is the difference between knowing something (maʿrifah) and believing in it (taṣdīq)?
b: Knowledge is recognizing and being aware of something, whereas taṣdīq is accepting and affirming that something is true in the heart.

f: How do some scholars define taṣdīq in relation to īmān?
b: They define taṣdīq as the heart attaching itself to what is known from the report of a truthful informer, with acceptance and submission.

f: Why is taṣdīq considered something acquired and voluntary according to some scholars?
b: Because a person can choose to seek evidence, reflect, direct attention, and remove obstacles that prevent acceptance. Therefore, he can be rewarded for attaining it.

f: Why is knowledge (maʿrifah) not sufficient by itself to constitute īmān?
b: Because knowledge may occur without choice or acceptance, such as a person seeing an object and immediately knowing what it is. Faith requires willing acceptance of the truth.

f: What difficulty arises regarding the claim that taṣdīq is voluntary?
b: The difficulty is that taṣdīq is a type of knowledge, and knowledge is an inner state of the soul rather than a direct voluntary action.

f: How is the difficulty regarding the voluntary nature of taṣdīq answered?
b: It is answered that although the state of affirmation itself is not directly created by choice, obtaining it occurs through voluntary actions such as seeking proofs, focusing attention, and removing barriers. This is why faith is considered acquired and subject to responsibility.

f: Why can a person not simply have knowledge and automatically be considered a believer?
b: Because knowledge alone may exist without acceptance. True faith requires the additional element of submission and affirmation, which is the meaning of taṣdīq.

f: According to the author, are īmān (faith) and islām (submission) the same?
b: Yes. The author states that īmān and islām are one because islām means submission and surrender through accepting Allah's commands, and this is the reality of heartly affirmation (taṣdīq).

f: Why does the author say that īmān and islām are the same in the Sharīʿah?
b: Because it is not correct in Islamic law to judge someone as being a believer but not a Muslim, or a Muslim but not a believer. The unity between them means that neither exists separately from the other in the legal sense.

f: Does the unity of īmān and islām mean that their definitions are identical?
b: Not necessarily. The scholars indicate that they are not different in the sense that one cannot exist without the other, rather than that their linguistic meanings are completely identical.

f: How do scholars explain the relationship between īmān and islām?
b: Īmān is believing in Allah's commands and prohibitions by affirming them, while islām is submitting and surrendering to Allah's authority. Submission cannot occur without accepting the commands and prohibitions, so īmān and islām cannot separate from each other legally.

f: What challenge is presented by those who claim that īmān and islām are different?
b: They are asked: What is the ruling of someone who has īmān but not islām, or islām but not īmān? If they assign different rulings to these cases, they must prove it; otherwise their claim of difference has no basis.

f: How is the verse about the Bedouins who said "We believe" used as an argument that islām and īmān differ?
b: The verse states: ﴿قَالَتِ الْأَعْرَابُ آمَنَّا قُلْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا أَسْلَمْنَا﴾, which appears to show that islām can exist without īmān.

f: How is the verse about the Bedouins answered?
b: The answer is that the islām mentioned in the verse means outward submission, not the complete Islamic submission recognized in the Sharīʿah. It is like someone who pronounces the testimony of faith without inward affirmation.

f: How is the hadith defining islām as testimony, prayer, zakāh, fasting, and pilgrimage answered?
b: The answer is that these acts are the fruits and signs of islām, not its inner reality. They indicate and demonstrate the faith that exists in the heart.

f: How does the hadith "Īmān has over seventy branches" support the relationship between īmān and islām?
b: It shows that some outward actions, such as removing harm from the road, are counted among the branches of īmān. This demonstrates that outward acts are connected to faith as its signs and fruits.

f: When may a person say "I am truly a believer"?
b: When the servant possesses true affirmation and acceptance, it is permissible for him to say that he is a true believer.

f: Why should a person avoid saying "I am a believer, if Allah wills" according to the author?
b: Because it may imply doubt regarding one's faith, even though it can have other meanings such as humility, entrusting one's final state to Allah, avoiding self-praise, or seeking blessing by mentioning Allah.

f: Why does the author say "I am a believer, if Allah wills" is disliked rather than forbidden?
b: Because if the statement is not intended to express doubt, there is no reason to declare it impermissible. Many early scholars, including some Companions and Tābiʿūn, held this view.

f: Why is saying "I am young, if Allah wills" different from saying "I am a believer, if Allah wills"?
b: Youth is not a matter of acquired actions, nor does it involve praising oneself or uncertainty about one's final state. Faith, however, relates to one's ultimate outcome and can involve concerns about remaining steadfast until death.

f: How do some scholars explain the permissibility of saying "I am a believer, if Allah wills"?
b: They explain that the servant possesses the reality of faith that removes disbelief, but the perfection of faith can vary in strength. The complete faith referred to in verses such as ﴿أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ حَقًّا﴾ depends upon Allah's will and one's final state.

f: Why do some scholars connect "if Allah wills" with faith to the person's final outcome?
b: Because true success depends on dying upon faith. A person may spend much of his life in disbelief but die as a believer, or spend much of his life as a believer but not remain steadfast until death.

f: What is the view of those who say that faith (īmān) neither increases nor decreases?
b: They argue that the reality of faith is the heart’s conviction (taṣdīq), which reaches the level of certainty and submission. Such conviction cannot increase or decrease; whether a person performs acts of obedience or commits sins, his conviction itself remains unchanged.

f: How do scholars explain the verses indicating that faith increases?
b: They explain them according to what Imām Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ said: people initially believed in general, then faith increased with each new obligation revealed, as they believed in each specific command. Thus, faith increased by the increase of things required to be believed in.

f: What criticism is made of the explanation that faith only increased during the Prophet’s ﷺ lifetime?
b: It is objected that learning the details of religious obligations is still possible after the Prophet’s ﷺ time. Faith is obligatory in a general manner regarding what is known generally and in detail regarding what is known in detail; detailed knowledge is clearly greater and more complete.

f: What is another explanation given for the increase of faith?
b: Some say that remaining firm and constant upon faith is an increase in faith because faith continues through time by the renewal of its likeness. This is criticized because obtaining something similar after something disappears is not truly an increase.

f: How do some scholars explain the increase and decrease of faith through actions?
b: They say the intended meaning is the increase of faith’s fruits, light, and illumination in the heart. It increases through righteous actions and decreases through sins.

f: Why is the increase and decrease of faith obvious according to those who include actions within faith?
b: Because if actions are considered part of faith itself, then faith naturally accepts increase and decrease, since actions themselves increase and decrease.

f: What argument do some scholars give that the reality of conviction (taṣdīq) can increase and decrease?
b: They argue that people’s convictions differ in strength. The conviction of ordinary believers is not equal to the conviction of the Prophet ﷺ. This is supported by the statement of Ibrāhīm عليه السلام: {وَلَكِنْ لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي}.

f: What is the difference between knowledge (maʿrifah) and conviction (taṣdīq) regarding faith?
b: Knowledge is merely knowing something, while conviction is the heart’s acceptance and affirmation of the truth of what is known. Knowledge may exist without submission or acceptance, whereas faith requires acceptance and affirmation.

f: Why is defining faith as mere knowledge incorrect?
b: Because some disbelievers possessed knowledge of the truth, such as the People of the Book who recognized the Prophet ﷺ, yet they were still disbelievers because they rejected him and refused to submit. Allah says: {وَجَحَدُوا بِهَا وَاسْتَيْقَنَتْهَا أَنْفُسُهُمْ}.

f: What is the definition of faith according to the scholars?
b: Faith is believing in the heart in everything that the Prophet ﷺ brought from Allah تَعَالَى that is necessarily known to be part of the religion.

f: Is detailed faith (īmān tafṣīlī) required for a person to be considered a believer?
b: No. General faith (īmān ijmālī) in what is necessarily known from the religion is sufficient for fulfilling the obligation of faith. Detailed faith is more complete but not required for the basic status of being a believer.

f: What is the view of scholars who say faith consists of both affirmation and declaration?
b: They say faith is the heart’s conviction and the tongue’s declaration. This was the view of some scholars, including Shams al-A’immah and Fakhr al-Islām.

f: What is the view of the majority of later scholars regarding the essence of faith?
b: The majority of scholars hold that the essence of faith is the heart’s conviction, while verbal declaration is a condition for worldly rulings because the heart’s conviction is hidden and requires an outward sign.

f: What is the ruling of someone who believes in the heart but cannot declare faith verbally?
b: Such a person is a believer before Allah, even though worldly rulings cannot necessarily be applied to him without outward declaration, as in the case of someone unable to speak.

f: What is the ruling of a hypocrite who declares faith with the tongue but does not believe in the heart?
b: He is the opposite: he is treated outwardly according to Islam, but before Allah he is not a believer because true faith requires heart conviction.

f: What evidences show that faith is in the heart?
b: Among them are Allah’s words: {أُولَئِكَ كَتَبَ فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْإِيمَانَ}, {وَقَلْبُهُ مُطْمَئِنٌّ بِالْإِيمَانِ}, and the Prophet’s ﷺ supplication: “O Allah, make my heart firm upon Your religion and obedience.”

f: Why is a mere verbal declaration not sufficient for true faith?
b: Because Allah described some people who said “we believe” but were not believers: {وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَقُولُ آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ... وَمَا هُمْ بِمُؤْمِنِينَ}. True faith requires heart acceptance.

f: What is the view of the majority regarding whether actions are part of the essence of faith?
b: The majority of theologians, hadith scholars, and jurists say faith consists of heart conviction, verbal declaration, and actions. However, they do not consider abandoning actions to remove a person from the basic reality of faith.

f: What evidence is given that actions are separate from the essence of faith?
b: The Qur’an frequently mentions faith and righteous deeds separately, such as: {إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ}. The conjunction indicates distinction between the two.

f: How do scholars respond to the argument that actions must be part of faith because they are mentioned with faith?
b: They respond that the conjunction indicates distinction, and that actions are fruits, requirements, or signs of faith rather than part of its essential definition.

f: What is the second issue regarding whether faith increases or decreases?
b: The issue is whether the essence of faith itself increases and decreases. Those who define faith as perfect heart conviction say it does not, while others argue that conviction varies in strength.

f: What was the belief of some Qadariyyah regarding faith?
b: Some Qadariyyah claimed that faith is merely knowledge (maʿrifah).

f: Why did scholars reject the view that faith is merely knowledge?
b: Because many disbelievers know the truth but do not believe. Knowledge alone does not produce submission and acceptance.

f: What is the difference between knowledge and conviction according to some scholars?
b: Knowledge may occur without choice, such as seeing a wall and knowing it is a wall. Conviction involves the heart accepting and affirming the truth of a report.

f: Are faith (īmān) and Islam considered identical?
b: Yes, according to the author, faith and Islam are one in the sense that a person cannot truly be considered a believer without being a Muslim or a Muslim without faith.

f: What does it mean that faith and Islam are one?
b: It means they are inseparable in legal judgment, not necessarily identical in linguistic meaning. Faith refers to believing in Allah’s revelation, while Islam refers to submission and obedience to Allah.

f: How is the verse {قَالَتِ الْأَعْرَابُ آمَنَّا قُلْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا أَسْلَمْنَا} explained?
b: It refers to outward submission (Islam) without inward faith. The Arabs had outwardly submitted but had not yet attained true inward conviction.

f: How is the hadith defining Islam through the five pillars reconciled with faith being heart conviction?
b: The five pillars are the outward manifestations and signs of Islam, not the complete inner reality of faith itself.

f: What is the ruling on saying “I am truly a believer, if Allah wills”?
b: It is better not to say this if it implies doubt about one’s current faith. However, if it is said out of humility, dependence on Allah, fear of one’s end, or seeking blessing, many early scholars allowed it.

f: Why did the author say “it is not appropriate” rather than “it is forbidden” to say “I am a believer, if Allah wills”?
b: Because the statement is not always prohibited. It may be acceptable when it does not indicate doubt but rather humility or fear of the final outcome.

f: What is the belief of some scholars regarding certainty of faith and the phrase “if Allah wills”?
b: They say the believer possesses the reality of faith that removes disbelief, but complete faith and salvation depend upon Allah’s will and the person’s final state.

f: What is the meaning of the statement “the fortunate may become unfortunate and the unfortunate may become fortunate”?
b: A person who was disbelieving may become a believer and attain happiness, while a believer may apostatize and become unfortunate.

f: Is change (such as becoming faithful or sinful) attributed to Allah’s essence or attributes?
b: No. Change occurs in created beings, not in Allah تَعَالَى or His attributes, because Allah is eternal and not subject to created changes.

f: What wisdom exists in sending messengers?
b: Sending messengers contains benefit and wisdom, as they clarify matters of worldly and eternal benefit that human intellects cannot fully determine alone.

f: Is sending messengers obligatory upon Allah in the sense of being imposed upon Him?
b: No. It is not an obligation imposed upon Allah تَعَالَى, but rather something necessitated by His wisdom and the benefits it contains.

f: Who denied the possibility or necessity of sending messengers?
b: The Samaniyyah and Brahmans denied the possibility or need for sending messengers, while some theologians considered it merely possible without necessity.

f: What roles do messengers have according to the author?
b: They give glad tidings to believers of Paradise and reward, warn disbelievers and sinners of punishment, and explain what people need regarding worldly and religious matters.

f: Why can human intellect alone not discover everything needed for religion?
b: Because many matters such as details of Paradise, Hell, methods of worship, and unseen realities cannot be independently known through intellect and senses alone.

f: What mercy of Allah is mentioned regarding sending messengers?
b: Allah sent messengers as a mercy to creation, as stated: {وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً لِلْعَالَمِينَ}.

f: How did Allah support the messengers in proving their truthfulness?
b: Allah supported them with miracles that broke normal patterns and demonstrated their truthfulness against those who denied them.

f: What is a miracle (muʿjizah)?
b: A miracle is an extraordinary event that occurs at the hands of someone claiming prophethood, accompanied by a challenge to opponents who are unable to produce anything similar.

f: Why are miracles necessary for proving prophethood?
b: Without miracles, there would be no decisive distinction between a true prophet and a liar claiming prophethood.

f: How does the occurrence of a miracle establish knowledge of a prophet’s truthfulness?
b: Allah normally creates certainty in people’s hearts after witnessing a miracle, just as He creates certainty through normal sensory experiences.

f: Does the possibility that a miracle could theoretically occur without Allah’s direct action invalidate its proof?
b: No. Possibility in itself does not prevent certainty, just as it is possible in itself that Mount Uhud could turn into gold, yet we know with certainty that it has not happened.

f: Who were the first and last of the prophets according to the author?
b: The first prophet was Ādam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ and the last prophet was Muḥammad ﷺ.

f: How is the prophethood of Ādam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ established?
b: It is established through revelation, as there was no prophet before him, and through the Sunnah and consensus. Denying his prophethood is disbelief.

f: How is the prophethood of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ established?
b: His prophethood is established through his claim of prophethood and the miracles he displayed. His claim is known through mass transmission (tawātur), and his miracles prove his truthfulness.

f: What is the first proof mentioned for the prophethood of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ?
b: The first proof is that he brought the speech of Allah (the Qur’an) and challenged the eloquent Arabs, despite their mastery of language, to produce even the shortest chapter like it, but they were unable to do so.

f: Why did the Arabs not respond to the Qur’an by producing something similar?
b: Despite their intense opposition and desire to defeat him, they abandoned verbal challenge and resorted instead to fighting with swords, proving their inability to imitate the Qur’an.

f: What does the inability of the Arabs to imitate the Qur’an prove?
b: It proves that the Qur’an is from Allah تَعَالَى and that the Prophet ﷺ was truthful in his claim of prophethood.

f: What is the second proof mentioned for the prophethood of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ?
b: The second proof is the numerous extraordinary events and miracles transmitted from him, whose general occurrence reached the level of tawātur even if individual details were transmitted through smaller chains.

f: What example does the author give to explain how a miracle can be established through tawātur?
b: He compares it to the courage of ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and the existence of Ḥātim al-Ṭā’ī; both are established through widespread transmission even though details of their stories may come through individual reports.

f: What additional proofs do people of spiritual insight use to prove the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ?
b: They consider the entirety of his life before prophethood, during his mission, and after it, including his noble character, wise rulings, steadfastness, trust in Allah, and victory over enemies despite their efforts to criticize him.

f: Why do the Prophet’s ﷺ character and life prove his prophethood?
b: Because it is impossible for someone who fabricates lies about Allah to possess such perfection, remain steadfast for twenty-three years, establish a religion, overcome enemies, and have his legacy preserved until the Day of Judgment.

f: What is another proof for the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ mentioned by the author?
b: That he appeared among a people without scripture or advanced wisdom, then taught them the Qur’an, wisdom, laws, and noble character, transforming many into people of intellectual and moral excellence.

f: What does the success and spread of Islam prove about Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ?
b: It proves his prophethood because Allah تَعَالَى supported and elevated his religion above all religions, as promised.

f: What proves that Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ is the final prophet?
b: The Qur’an and his own words indicate that he is the Seal of the Prophets and was sent to all people, including jinn and humans.

f: Was Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ’s ﷺ prophethood limited to the Arabs?
b: No. His prophethood is universal for all humanity. The author rejects the claim of some Christians that his mission was only for Arabs.

f: How is the descent of ʿĪsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ after Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ reconciled with him being the final prophet?
b: ʿĪsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ will follow the law of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ. His previous law has been abrogated, and he will not bring new revelation or establish new rulings; he will act as a follower of the Prophet ﷺ.

f: Who will lead the prayer when ʿĪsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ descends according to the preferred view mentioned?
b: The Mahdī will lead the prayer because he is from the Ummah of Muḥammad ﷺ, and ʿĪsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ will follow him.

f: How many prophets are reported in some narrations?
b: Some narrations mention 124,000 prophets, while another narration mentions 224,000 prophets.

f: Why does the author say it is better not to rely on a specific number of prophets?
b: Because Allah تعالى says: {مِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَصَصْنَا عَلَيْكَ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ لَمْ نَقْصُصْ عَلَيْكَ} — some prophets were mentioned and others were not.

f: Why should a specific number of prophets not be accepted from isolated reports?
b: Because individual reports (khabar al-wāḥid), even with proper conditions, only produce probability in matters of belief, especially when there are differences in narrations and the report conflicts with the apparent meaning of the Qur’an.

f: What problem arises from accepting a specific number of prophets from a weak report?
b: It could lead to including someone who was not a prophet or excluding someone who was a prophet, if the exact number is assumed to be fixed.

f: What qualities did all prophets possess according to the author?
b: All prophets were truthful informers, trustworthy conveyers of Allah’s message, and sincere advisors to creation.

f: Why must prophets be truthful and trustworthy?
b: Because otherwise the purpose of sending messengers would be defeated.

f: Are prophets protected from lying?
b: Yes. They are protected from lying, especially in matters of conveying revelation, religious rulings, and guiding their communities.

f: Are prophets protected from all sins according to the author?
b: No. There is detail: they are protected from disbelief absolutely, from intentionally committing major sins according to the majority, and there are differences regarding minor sins.

f: Are prophets protected from disbelief before and after revelation?
b: Yes. The author states there is consensus that prophets are protected from disbelief both before and after receiving revelation.

f: What is the majority view regarding prophets intentionally committing major sins?
b: The majority hold that prophets are protected from intentionally committing major sins, unlike some groups who disagreed.

f: What is the disagreement regarding prophets committing major sins unintentionally?
b: The majority allow that such things could occur unintentionally, though they differ regarding the evidence for this prohibition.

f: What is the majority view regarding prophets intentionally committing minor sins?
b: The majority allow the possibility of minor sins intentionally, unlike al-Jubbā’ī and his followers, though matters that indicate lowliness or disgrace are excluded.

f: Can prophets commit minor sins unintentionally?
b: Yes. This is accepted by agreement, except for actions that indicate disgrace or dishonor.

f: What condition do scholars place regarding prophets committing minor mistakes?
b: They must be alerted to them and then cease from them.

f: What is the view of the Muʿtazilah regarding prophets committing sins before revelation?
b: They held that prophets could not commit major sins before revelation because it would cause people to dislike them and prevent the purpose of sending them.

f: How does the author respond to the Muʿtazilah regarding sins before revelation?
b: He rejects the idea that all sins cause rejection, but accepts that acts causing humiliation or repulsion, such as disgraceful behavior, would be impossible for prophets.

f: What types of sins are definitely impossible for prophets according to the author?
b: Disbelief, disgraceful immoral acts, and actions that would repel people from accepting their message.

f: What is the ruling on reports about prophets that suggest they committed lies or sins?
b: Reports transmitted through solitary chains (āḥād) are rejected if they contradict the established doctrine of prophetic infallibility. Reports transmitted through mass transmission (tawātur), if their apparent meaning can be interpreted, are interpreted away; otherwise, they are understood as referring to leaving what is more appropriate (tark al-awlā) or events before prophethood.

f: What is the ruling on Prophet Muhammad ﷺ compared to the other prophets?
b: Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is the best and most excellent of all prophets.

f: What evidence is given that Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is the best of the prophets?
b: The verse: ﴿كُنتُمْ خَيْرَ أُمَّةٍ﴾ indicates the superiority of his الأمة, and the excellence of a nation is connected to the perfection of its prophet. Therefore, the perfection of Muhammad ﷺ shows his superiority over other prophets.

f: Why is the hadith “I am the master of the children of Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, and there is no pride in it” not sufficient as evidence that Muhammad ﷺ is superior to Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ?
b: Because it proves that he is superior to the descendants of Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, but it does not explicitly prove superiority over Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ himself.

f: What is the belief regarding angels?
b: Angels are servants of Allah who act according to His command.

f: What Quranic evidence proves that angels obey Allah completely?
b: Allah says: ﴿لَا يَسْبِقُونَهُ بِالْقَوْلِ وَهُمْ بِأَمْرِهِ يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ and ﴿لَا يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ عَنْ عِبَادَتِهِ وَلَا يَسْتَحْسِرُونَ﴾.

f: Can angels be described as male or female?
b: They cannot be described as male or female unless there is transmitted revelation or rational proof.

f: Why is the belief that angels are daughters of Allah rejected?
b: Because it is false and combines belittling Allah by attributing offspring to Him while also elevating angels incorrectly.

f: How do the claims of idolaters and Jews regarding angels differ?
b: Idolaters exaggerated the status of angels by claiming they were Allah’s daughters, while Jews diminished them by claiming angels could commit disbelief and be punished for it.

f: Was Iblis one of the angels?
b: No. The author states that Iblis was from the jinn, not an angel. His being mentioned with angels in the story of Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ is because he was among those associated with them in worship.

f: How is Iblis’ exclusion from the command to prostrate to Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ understood?
b: The exception in the verse is understood as an exception referring to those present with the angels, not necessarily one of the angels themselves; therefore, Iblis being from the jinn is not problematic.

f: What is the correct view regarding Hārūt and Mārūt?
b: The author states that the stronger view is that they were two angels who did not commit disbelief or major sins. Their punishment was a form of admonition, similar to how prophets may be admonished for minor slips.

f: Did Hārūt and Mārūt commit disbelief by teaching magic?
b: No. Teaching magic itself is not disbelief; disbelief occurs through believing in magic or practicing it in a manner involving false beliefs.

f: What are the books revealed by Allah to His prophets?
b: They are books containing Allah’s commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings.

f: Are the revealed books multiple forms of Allah’s speech or multiple speeches?
b: Allah’s speech is one and eternal; the differences are in the forms of recitation, wording, and written expressions.

f: Which revealed book is considered the greatest in terms of recitation and benefit?
b: The Qur’an is the greatest, followed by the Torah, the Gospel (Injīl), and the Psalms (Zabūr).

f: Why can some Qur’anic chapters be considered superior to others?
b: Although Allah’s speech itself is one and cannot be divided in excellence, some chapters can be superior due to greater benefit, reward of recitation, or containing more mention of Allah.

f: What happened to the previous revealed books after the Qur’an was revealed?
b: Their recitation, writing, and some rulings were abrogated by the Qur’an.

f: What is the belief regarding the Miʿrāj (Ascension) of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ?
b: The Miʿrāj is true: Prophet Muhammad ﷺ ascended physically while awake from the Sacred Mosque to the heavens and beyond, by Allah’s power.

f: What is the evidence for the Miʿrāj?
b: It is established through widely transmitted reports (khabar mashhūr), and denying it is considered an innovation.

f: Why is the claim that the Miʿrāj is impossible rejected?
b: Because it relies on philosophical assumptions. Allah is capable of all possible things, and physical movement through the heavens is rationally possible.

f: Why does the author emphasize that the Miʿrāj occurred while Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was awake?
b: To refute those who claimed it was only a dream, such as reports attributed to Muʿāwiyah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: What verse is used regarding the vision shown to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ?
b: Allah says: ﴿وَمَا جَعَلْنَا الرُّؤْيَا الَّتِي أَرَيْنَاكَ إِلَّا فِتْنَةً لِّلنَّاسِ﴾.

f: How is the claim that the Miʿrāj was only a spiritual journey answered?
b: The answer is that the Miʿrāj was with both the body and the soul. The phrase بِشَخْصِهِ indicates that it occurred with the Prophet ﷺ himself, not merely his soul.

f: Was the Miʿrāj in a dream or only spiritual form something that must be completely rejected?
b: No. A spiritual or dream experience of Miʿrāj is not something inherently impossible, but the author rejects limiting it to that.

f: Why did the disbelievers strongly reject the Miʿrāj?
b: Because they understood the claim as a physical journey and considered it impossible, and some Muslims even apostatized due to their inability to accept it.

f: What does the phrase “إِلَى السَّمَاءِ” in discussions of the Miʿrāj indicate?
b: It indicates disagreement among the early scholars regarding the final destination of the Miʿrāj. Some said Paradise, some said the Throne, some said beyond the Throne, and others said the edge of creation.

f: What is the difference in certainty between the Isrāʾ and the Miʿrāj?
b: The Isrāʾ (journey from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām to al-Masjid al-Aqṣā) is certain because it is established by the Qur’an. The Miʿrāj from earth to the heavens is established by well-known reports. Details beyond the heavens are based on solitary reports.

f: Did Prophet Muhammad ﷺ see Allah during the Miʿrāj with his physical eyes?
b: The correct view according to the author is that he saw Allah with his heart (fuʾād), not with his physical eyes.

f: What are the karāmāt (miracles) of the awliyāʾ (saints)?
b: They are real occurrences of extraordinary events appearing through a righteous servant of Allah without a claim of prophethood.

f: Who is considered a walī (friend of Allah) according to the author?
b: A walī is someone who knows Allah and His attributes, remains devoted to obedience, avoids sins, and refrains from excessive indulgence in desires.

f: What distinguishes a karāmah from a muʿjizah (prophetic miracle)?
b: A karāmah occurs through a righteous person without a claim of prophethood. A muʿjizah occurs with someone claiming prophethood.

f: What is the difference between a true karāmah and istidrāj (gradual deception)?
b: A true karāmah is accompanied by faith and righteous deeds. An extraordinary event without faith and obedience is considered istidrāj.

f: What evidence proves the reality of karāmāt of the awliyāʾ?
b: Numerous karāmāt are transmitted from the Companions and later generations through widespread reports, making their denial impossible. The Qur’an also mentions extraordinary events involving Maryam and the companion of Sulaymān عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ.

f: Why is there no need to prove the possibility of karāmāt after their occurrence is established?
b: Because actual occurrence already proves possibility. Once something is known to happen, there is no need to separately establish that it could happen.

f: What example is given of a karāmah involving travel over a great distance?
b: The example is Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, the companion of Sulaymān عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, who brought the throne of Bilqīs before Sulaymān عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ could blink.

f: What example is given of provision appearing miraculously for a walī?
b: The example is Maryam عَلَيْهَا السَّلَامُ, who found provision with her whenever Zakariyyā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ entered her chamber.

f: What examples are given of walking on water as a karāmah?
b: The author mentions reports of some awliyāʾ walking on water.

f: What examples are given of animals or inanimate objects speaking?
b: Examples include the speaking of a bowl that glorified Allah in the presence of Sulaymān عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ and Abū al-Dardāʾ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and animals speaking such as the dog of the Companions of the Cave and the cow that spoke to a man.

f: What was the karāmah of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ mentioned in the text?
b: While giving a sermon in Madinah, he saw the Muslim army in Nahāwand from afar and warned its commander Sāriyah by calling: “O Sāriyah, the mountain!” The commander heard him despite the great distance.

f: What other examples of karāmāt are mentioned from the Companions?
b: The author mentions Khālid ibn al-Walīd رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ drinking poison without being harmed, and the flowing of the Nile by the written command of ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: What objection did the Muʿtazilah raise against the karāmāt of awliyāʾ?
b: They argued that if extraordinary events could occur through saints, they would become confused with prophetic miracles, making it impossible to distinguish prophets from others.

f: How did the author answer the Muʿtazilah objection that karāmāt of awliyāʾ would confuse people between saints and prophets?
b: He answered that the karāmah of a wali is itself a miracle for the prophet whom the wali follows, because it proves that the wali is truthful in following that prophet.

f: Why is a karāmah of a wali considered a miracle for the prophet he follows?
b: Because the karāmah shows that the person is truly a wali, and someone cannot be a true wali unless he believes in the prophet’s message, accepts it, and follows his commands and prohibitions.

f: Can a person be a wali while rejecting the prophet’s teachings or claiming independence from the prophet?
b: No. If someone claimed independence and refused to follow the prophet, he would not be a wali and no karāmah would appear through him.

f: What is the relationship between a prophet’s muʿjizah and a wali’s karāmah?
b: The same extraordinary event can be considered a muʿjizah for the prophet and a karāmah for the wali. For the prophet it proves prophethood, while for the wali it proves his righteousness and following of the prophet.

f: What distinguishes a prophet when a miracle occurs from a wali when a karāmah occurs?
b: A prophet knows he is a prophet, intends to show the miracle as proof, and decisively judges according to it. A wali does not necessarily know beforehand, intend it, or make such a claim.

f: Who is the best of mankind after Prophet Muhammad ﷺ according to the author?
b: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ is the best of mankind after Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

f: Why does the author say “after our Prophet” instead of “after the prophets”?
b: He means temporal succession, since there is no prophet after Muhammad ﷺ. However, ʿĪsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ must be excluded because he will return after Muhammad ﷺ.

f: Why does the phrase “after every human being after our Prophet” require qualification?
b: Because if it included every human who exists after Muhammad ﷺ, it would conflict with ʿĪsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ. If it meant everyone born after him, it would not prove superiority over the Companions.

f: Why is Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ considered superior to all other humans after Prophet Muhammad ﷺ?
b: Because he immediately and without hesitation affirmed the Prophet ﷺ, believed in his prophethood, and accepted the Miʿrāj without doubt.

f: Why is ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ ranked after Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ?
b: Because he was al-Fārūq, the one who distinguished truth from falsehood in judgments and disputes.

f: Why is ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ called Dhū al-Nūrayn (the possessor of two lights)?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ married him to his daughter Ruqayyah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا, and after her death married him to his daughter Umm Kulthūm رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا.

f: What did the Prophet ﷺ say regarding ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ marrying another daughter?
b: He said: “If I had a third daughter, I would have married her to you as well.”

f: What is the author’s position regarding the ranking of ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ?
b: He states that the early scholars differed and some withheld judgment. He notes that if superiority means greater reward, there is room for discussion, but if it means the number of recognized virtues, there is no doubt.

f: What evidence does the author mention for the order of the first four caliphs?
b: The Companions agreed upon the succession of Abū Bakr, then ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān, then ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ.

f: Why does the author argue that Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ’s caliphate was legitimate?
b: Because the Companions gathered after the Prophet’s ﷺ death, discussed the matter, agreed upon Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and pledged allegiance to him.

f: Why does the author argue that ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ accepted Abū Bakr’s رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ caliphate?
b: Because ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ pledged allegiance to Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and did not oppose him, even though he would have had evidence to argue if there had been a specific prophetic appointment for himself.

f: How does the author respond to the claim that the Companions abandoned a clear text appointing ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ as caliph?
b: He argues that it is impossible that the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ would collectively agree upon falsehood and abandon a clear command.

f: How was ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ appointed as caliph after Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ?
b: Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ dictated his written appointment of ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ wrote it down. The document was presented to the people, and they pledged allegiance to ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: What is the ruling on the order of preference among the prophets?
b: The best of the prophets is Muhammad ﷺ. The superiority of his nation is due to the perfection of its religion, which follows from the perfection of their Prophet.

f: Who is considered the best human after Prophet Muhammad ﷺ according to the Hanafi theologians?
b: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ is considered the best human after Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, followed by Umar al-Faruq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, then Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ Dhun-Nurayn, then Ali al-Murtada رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ.

f: Why is Abu Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ considered the best after Prophet Muhammad ﷺ?
b: Because he immediately affirmed the Prophet’s ﷺ prophethood without hesitation and believed him during the Mi‘raj without doubt.

f: Why is Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ called al-Faruq?
b: He is called al-Faruq because he distinguished between truth and falsehood in judgments and disputes.

f: Why is Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ called Dhun-Nurayn?
b: He is called Dhun-Nurayn because the Prophet ﷺ married him to two of his daughters, Ruqayyah and then Umm Kulthum رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا.

f: What is the position regarding the superiority of Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ over Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ?
b: The early scholars differed regarding the preference of Uthman and Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا. The author states that if superiority means greater reward there is room for discussion, but if it means greater recognizable virtues, Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ has precedence.

f: What is the order of the rightly guided caliphate according to the author?
b: The caliphate followed the same order: Abu Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Uthman, then Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ.

f: Why is Abu Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ’s caliphate considered valid?
b: The Companions agreed upon his caliphate after consultation, and Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ gave him allegiance. If there had been a clear text appointing Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, he would have opposed it.

f: Why is Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ’s caliphate considered valid?
b: Abu Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ appointed Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ after consulting the Companions, and they accepted his leadership.

f: Why is Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ’s caliphate considered valid?
b: Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ left the matter to a council of six Companions, who appointed Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and the Companions accepted his leadership.

f: Why is Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ’s caliphate considered valid?
b: After Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ was martyred, the leading Muhajirun and Ansar requested Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ to accept the caliphate because he was the most suitable person of his time.

f: How does the author explain the conflicts that occurred among the Companions during Ali’s رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ caliphate?
b: They were not due to denial of Ali’s رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ legitimacy as caliph, but were the result of differing ijtihad and interpretations.

f: What is the meaning of the statement: “The caliphate is thirty years, then after it there is kingship and leadership”?
b: It means the complete caliphate free from opposition and deviation lasted thirty years after the Prophet ﷺ. Later rulers may still have had authority and legitimacy, but not the same complete form.

f: Is appointing an imam (leader) obligatory according to the author?
b: Yes, the scholars agreed that appointing an imam is obligatory. The disagreement is whether the obligation is upon Allah or upon people; the Hanafi position is that it is obligatory upon people through revelation.

f: What evidence is given for the obligation of appointing an imam?
b: The hadith: “Whoever dies without knowing the imam of his time dies the death of ignorance,” and the fact that the Companions prioritized appointing a leader after the Prophet ﷺ before his burial.

f: Why is appointing an imam necessary for Muslims?
b: Many religious duties depend upon leadership, such as implementing rulings, establishing punishments, protecting borders, organizing armies, collecting charity, resolving disputes, accepting testimony, and arranging public religious matters.

f: Why is one powerful person in each region not sufficient instead of a single imam?
b: Because this would lead to disputes and disorder in religious and worldly affairs. A general leader prevents conflicts and preserves the religion.

f: Why is worldly authority alone insufficient without an imam?
b: A powerful ruler may maintain worldly order, but the more important purpose is maintaining religious order through implementation of Allah’s law.

f: What are the conditions of the miracles given to prophets?
b: Prophetic miracles are extraordinary events that occur at the hands of a person claiming prophethood and challenge opponents in a way that they cannot imitate.

f: Why are miracles necessary for proving prophethood?
b: Without miracles, people would not be obligated to accept a prophet’s claim, and there would be no clear distinction between a true prophet and a liar.

f: How does the Qur’an prove the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ according to the author?
b: The Qur’an is the speech of Allah revealed through him ﷺ. The Arabs, despite their unmatched eloquence and strong motivation to oppose him, were unable to produce even a short chapter like it.

f: What other evidence proves the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ?
b: Numerous extraordinary events transmitted through widespread reports, along with his noble character, wisdom, steadfastness, and success in establishing Islam.

f: Why is Muhammad ﷺ the final prophet?
b: Because Allah revealed in the Qur’an that he is the Seal of the Prophets and sent him to all people, including jinn and humans.

f: How is the descent of Isa عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ after Muhammad ﷺ explained?
b: Isa عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ will follow Muhammad ﷺ’s law and will not bring a new revelation or independent legislation.

f: How many prophets were there according to some narrations?
b: Some narrations mention 124,000 prophets, while others mention 224,000. The author says it is better not to rely on a specific number because Allah says that some messengers were mentioned and others were not.

f: Are prophets truthful and trustworthy?
b: Yes. All prophets were truthful, trustworthy, and conveyed Allah’s message. They are protected from lying, especially in conveying revelation and religious rulings.

f: Are prophets protected from major sins?
b: According to the majority of scholars, prophets are protected from disbelief and intentional major sins, though there are detailed discussions regarding minor sins and actions before prophethood.

f: How are reports that appear to attribute sins or lies to prophets treated?
b: Reports transmitted through solitary chains are rejected if they contradict prophetic infallibility. Authentic reports are interpreted appropriately, such as referring to leaving what is preferable or events before prophethood.

f: What is the belief regarding angels?
b: Angels are servants of Allah who obey His commands and never precede Him in speech or disobey His orders.

f: Are angels described as male or female?
b: Angels are not described as male or female unless there is revelation proving it. Claims that angels are daughters of Allah are false.

f: Was Iblis an angel?
b: According to the author, Iblis was from the jinn, not an angel. His being among the angels in worship allowed the command addressing angels to include him metaphorically.

f: What is the belief regarding the revealed books?
b: Allah revealed books to His prophets containing His commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings. They are all Allah’s speech, though they differ in their written and recited forms.

f: Which revealed books are considered superior in order?
b: The Qur’an is superior, followed by the Torah, the Gospel, and the Zabur, due to the superiority of their revealed forms and benefits.

f: What is the belief regarding the Mi‘raj of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ?
b: The Mi‘raj was a real journey of the Prophet ﷺ with his body and soul while awake, from the Sacred Mosque to the heavens and beyond what Allah willed.

f: What part of the Night Journey is established by the Qur’an?
b: The Isra from Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa is established definitively by the Qur’an. The ascent through the heavens is established by famous reports.

f: What is the belief regarding the Prophet ﷺ seeing Allah during the Mi‘raj?
b: The correct view is that he ﷺ saw Allah with his heart, not with his physical eyes.

f: What are the karamat (miracles) of the saints?
b: Karamat are extraordinary events appearing through a righteous servant of Allah without a claim of prophethood.

f: What distinguishes a karamah from a miracle of a prophet?
b: A miracle accompanies a claim of prophethood, while a karamah occurs from a true follower of a prophet without claiming independent revelation.

f: Why do miracles of saints not conflict with prophetic miracles?
b: A saint’s miracle actually proves the truth of the prophet he follows, because a true saint must believe in and obey the prophet.

f: What are examples of karamat mentioned by the author?
b: Examples include Maryam receiving provision from Allah, Asif ibn Barkhiya bringing the throne of Bilqis, walking on water, speaking with animals or inanimate objects, Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ’s call to Sariyah, and other extraordinary events.

f: What is one of the conditions of an imam (Muslim ruler) regarding his visibility?
b: The imam should be apparent and accessible to the people so they can refer to him, and he can fulfill the purposes for which leadership was established.

f: Why should the imam not be hidden from the people?
b: Because hiding prevents the imam from managing public interests and fulfilling his responsibilities.

f: Why should the imam not be someone awaited in the future?
b: Because leadership must exist in the present to maintain religion and worldly affairs, not depend on the appearance of a future figure when conditions improve.

f: Which group believes that the true imam after Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a hidden imam?
b: The Imamiyyah Shi‘ah believe that after the Prophet ﷺ the rightful imams were Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and his descendants, ending with Muhammad al-Qa’im al-Mahdi, who they believe is hidden and will return.

f: How does the author respond to the idea of a hidden imam?
b: He argues that an absent imam cannot achieve the purposes of leadership. Fear from enemies may justify hiding a claim of leadership, but not complete disappearance from the people.

f: Why would people need an imam more during times of corruption and oppression?
b: Because when disorder increases and opinions differ, people have greater need for guidance and are more likely to submit to a just leader.

f: Must the imam be from Quraysh?
b: According to the author, yes. The imam must be Qurayshi, based on the hadith: “The imams are from Quraysh.”

f: Is the requirement that the imam be Qurayshi based only on a solitary narration?
b: Although the hadith is solitary, Abu Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ used it as evidence against the Ansar, and no one rejected it, so it became an accepted consensus.

f: Who disagreed with the requirement that the imam be Qurayshi?
b: The Khawarij and some Mu‘tazilah disagreed.

f: Must the imam be from Banu Hashim or the descendants of Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ?
b: No. The author states that being Qurayshi is required, but not being Hashimi or Alawi.

f: How does the author prove that the imam does not need to be Hashimi?
b: Because Abu Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Umar, and Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ were Qurayshi but not from Banu Hashim, and they were accepted as caliphs.

f: Who are considered Banu Hashim?
b: They are the descendants of Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, including the Alawiyyun (descendants of Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ) and Abbasiyyun (descendants of Abbas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ).

f: Why is Abu Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ Qurayshi?
b: Because he descended from Abu Quhafah, from the Qurayshi lineage.

f: Why is Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ Qurayshi?
b: Because he descended from al-Khattab ibn Nufayl from the Banu ‘Adi branch of Quraysh.

f: Why is Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ Qurayshi?
b: Because he descended from Uthman ibn Affan ibn Abi al-‘As رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ from Banu Umayyah of Quraysh.

f: Is it a condition that the imam be infallible (‘ma‘sūm)?
b: No. The author states that infallibility is not a condition for the imam.

f: What evidence do opponents give for requiring an infallible imam?
b: They cite Allah’s statement: {My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers} (Qur’an 2:124), arguing that a non-infallible person is a wrongdoer.

f: How does the author respond to the argument that every non-infallible person is a wrongdoer?
b: He says wrongdoing refers to a person who commits a sin that removes uprightness and does not repent, not every person who lacks infallibility.

f: What is the definition of ‘ismah (infallibility)?
b: It is a special divine favor by which Allah does not create sin in a servant, while the servant still retains ability and choice, encouraging obedience and preventing evil.

f: Does infallibility remove human choice?
b: No. The servant remains capable of choosing, which is why testing and reward remain meaningful.

f: Why is it incorrect to say that an infallible person is physically unable to sin?
b: Because if sin were impossible for him, abandoning sin would not be a meaningful act of obedience and he would not deserve reward for avoiding it.

f: Must the imam be the most virtuous person of his time?
b: No. The imam does not have to be superior to everyone of his era.

f: Why does the imam not need to be the most virtuous person?
b: A person with less virtue may still have better knowledge of political matters, greater ability to govern, or may prevent greater conflict.

f: Why did Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ appoint a council of six for choosing the next caliph?
b: Because although they differed in virtue, all were capable of leadership, and choosing among them prevented conflict.

f: How can choosing an imam by a council be allowed if appointing two imams at once is forbidden?
b: Two independent imams are forbidden because their commands could conflict. In a council, they function collectively as one decision-making body.

f: What does it mean that the imam must have complete authority (wilayah)?
b: It means he must be a Muslim, free, male, sane, and mature, possessing full legal authority.

f: Why is a non-Muslim not eligible to be imam?
b: Because Allah has not given the disbelievers authority over believers.

f: Why is a slave not eligible to be imam according to the author?
b: Because he is occupied with serving his master and is viewed as lacking independent authority.

f: Why is a woman not eligible to be imam according to the author?
b: The author cites traditional arguments regarding leadership responsibilities, mentioning deficiencies in certain areas of legal authority.

f: Why is a child or insane person not eligible to be imam?
b: Because they lack the ability to manage public affairs and make independent decisions.

f: What abilities must an imam possess?
b: He must be capable of managing Muslim affairs, implementing rulings, protecting Islamic lands, and establishing justice.

f: What does the imam need in order to protect society?
b: He needs knowledge, justice, competence, strength, courage, and the ability to distinguish between the oppressed and the oppressor.

f: Does an imam lose his position because of sinfulness (fisq)?
b: According to the author, no. The imam does not become removed merely because he commits sins.

f: Why does the author say a sinful imam is not automatically removed?
b: Because after the rightly guided caliphs, some rulers displayed wrongdoing, yet the early scholars continued obeying them, praying behind them, and maintaining social order.

f: Does an imam lose his position due to sinfulness (fisq) according to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ?
b: No. According to Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, an imam does not become removed merely because of fisq or injustice, because the Companions and early scholars continued praying behind sinful rulers and did not rebel against them.

f: Why does Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ not remove a sinful imam?
b: Because infallibility is not a condition for becoming imam in the first place, so remaining in the position is even more appropriate. Removing him could also cause greater harm and disorder.

f: What is Imam al-Shafi‘i’s position regarding a sinful imam?
b: Imam al-Shafi‘i رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ holds that an imam becomes removed due to fisq and injustice, just as a judge or governor does.

f: Why does Imam al-Shafi‘i رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ argue that a sinful person is not suitable for authority?
b: Because a sinful person cannot be trusted to manage others when he cannot even properly manage himself.

f: What is Abu Hanifah’s رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ evidence that a sinful person may still hold authority?
b: Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ considers a sinful person to remain among those eligible for authority, demonstrated by allowing a sinful father to arrange the marriage of his minor daughter.

f: What is the distinction between a sinful judge and a sinful imam according to the Shafi‘i school?
b: A sinful judge is removed, but a sinful imam is not removed because removing an imam may cause rebellion and widespread conflict due to his power and influence.

f: What is the ruling on praying behind any righteous or sinful Muslim?
b: Prayer is valid behind every righteous or sinful Muslim, as long as the person’s sin does not reach disbelief.

f: What evidence is given for praying behind sinful leaders?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “Pray behind every righteous person,” and the scholars of the Ummah prayed behind sinful people and innovators without rejecting their prayers.

f: How are reports from some early scholars forbidding prayer behind sinners or innovators understood?
b: They are understood as referring to dislike (karahah), not invalidity, because praying behind such people is disliked but still valid.

f: When is prayer behind someone not permissible?
b: If the person’s sin or innovation reaches the level of disbelief (kufr), then praying behind him is not permissible.

f: Why did the Mu‘tazilah allow prayer behind sinful people despite considering them outside true faith?
b: Because they considered the condition for leading prayer to be absence of disbelief, not necessarily possessing complete faith consisting of belief, declaration, and actions.

f: Should Muslims pray the funeral prayer over every righteous and sinful Muslim?
b: Yes, if the person died upon faith (iman), Muslims pray over him regardless of whether he was righteous or sinful.

f: What evidence is given for praying over sinful Muslims after death?
b: The consensus of Muslims and the hadith: “Do not abandon the prayer for anyone who dies from the people of the qiblah.”

f: Why are discussions about prayer behind sinners and views about the Companions mentioned in a book of theology?
b: Because they are issues distinguishing Ahl al-Sunnah from other groups such as the Mu‘tazilah, Shi‘ah, philosophers, and innovators, even if some issues are related to practical law.

f: What is the Sunni position regarding mentioning the Companions?
b: Muslims should refrain from mentioning the Companions except with goodness.

f: What evidence is given for avoiding criticism of the Companions?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not insult my Companions. If one of you spent the amount of Mount Uhud in gold, he would not reach even a mudd or half a mudd of one of them.”

f: Why are the Companions given such a high status?
b: Because they accompanied the Prophet ﷺ, supported him, witnessed revelation, and sacrificed greatly for Islam.

f: What did the Prophet ﷺ say about honoring the Companions?
b: He ﷺ said: “Honor my Companions, for they are the best of you.”

f: What is the ruling on insulting or attacking the Companions?
b: If the insult contradicts definitive religious evidence, such as accusing Aisha رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا of adultery, it is disbelief. Otherwise, it is considered innovation and sin.

f: How should Muslims view disagreements and conflicts that occurred among the Companions?
b: They should interpret them with valid explanations and avoid condemning the Companions, as their disagreements were based on sincere reasoning and interpretation.

f: What is the Sunni view regarding Mu‘awiyah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and those who fought with him?
b: The early scholars and righteous predecessors did not permit cursing Mu‘awiyah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ or his supporters. Their actions are understood as resulting from ijtihad, even if one side was mistaken.

f: Why did the author say the matter of disputes among the Companions should be left to Allah?
b: Because the Companions had great virtues, and judging their disputes requires caution and humility before Allah.

f: Why does the author say that the appearance of miracles (khawāriq al-ʿādāt) from saints does not create confusion between a saint and a prophet?
b: The miracles of saints are themselves a miracle for the Messenger ﷺ whose follower that saint is. A saint is only recognized as a saint because he affirms the Messenger’s ﷺ message and follows him. If he claimed independence from the Prophet ﷺ and did not follow him, he would not be a saint and such a miracle would not appear from him.

f: What is the difference between a prophet’s miracle and a saint’s karāmah?
b: A miracle for a prophet occurs with his knowledge that he is a prophet, his intention to show a sign, and his certainty regarding what the miracle proves. A saint’s karāmah occurs without a claim of prophethood and without him necessarily intending to display a supernatural event.

f: Who are the best of mankind after our Prophet ﷺ?
b: The best of mankind after our Prophet ﷺ are Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, then ʿUmar al-Fārūq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, then ʿUthmān Dhū al-Nūrayn, then ʿAlī al-Murtaḍā رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ.

f: Why is it better to say “after the prophets” rather than “after our Prophet” when discussing the best humans?
b: Saying “after the prophets” is more precise because if one says “after our Prophet” without qualification, it could include ʿĪsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, who will return after our Prophet ﷺ.

f: Why is Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ considered the first among mankind after the Prophet ﷺ?
b: Because he immediately affirmed the Prophet ﷺ in his prophethood without hesitation and also believed in the Miʿrāj without doubt.

f: Why is ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ considered second among mankind after the Prophet ﷺ?
b: Because he was al-Fārūq, the one who distinguished truth from falsehood in judgments and disputes.

f: Why is ʿUthmān رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ given the third position?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ married his daughters Ruqayyah and then Umm Kulthūm to him, earning him the title Dhū al-Nūrayn (the possessor of two lights).

f: What is the position of ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ in the ranking of the Companions?
b: He is fourth among the greatest Companions according to the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah. The author notes that if superiority means greater reward, there may be room for discussion, but if it means the qualities people recognize as virtues, there is no doubt.

f: Why does the author mention that the Companions differed about the superiority of ʿUthmān and ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا?
b: Because the early Muslims differed in this matter, although they agreed on the superiority of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا and on loving both ʿUthmān and ʿAlī.

f: Why was Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ chosen as the first caliph?
b: After the Prophet ﷺ passed away, the Companions gathered at Saqīfah Banī Sāʿidah, consulted each other, agreed upon Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and pledged allegiance to him. Even ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ later pledged allegiance, demonstrating agreement among the Companions.

f: Why does the author reject the Shīʿī claim that ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ was explicitly appointed as caliph by the Prophet ﷺ?
b: Because if such a clear appointment existed, ʿAlī رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ would have argued with Muʿāwiyah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ using it, and the Companions would not have agreed upon Abū Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ.

f: What is meant by the statement “the caliphate is thirty years, then after it comes kingship and authority”?
b: It refers to the complete and perfect caliphate that is free from shortcomings and opposition. It does not mean that every ruler after the Rightly Guided Caliphs lacks all authority or leadership.

f: Why is appointing an imam (leader) considered obligatory?
b: Because many religious obligations depend upon leadership, such as implementing legal rulings, establishing punishments, protecting borders, preparing armies, collecting charity, resolving disputes, accepting testimony, arranging marriages for those without guardians, and distributing spoils.

f: Is appointing an imam obligatory upon Allah or upon people?
b: According to the author, it is obligatory upon people based on revelation (samʿ), because the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever dies without knowing the imam of his time dies a death of ignorance.

f: Why is one general imam needed instead of multiple local rulers?
